fuentes/ultimatum-austrohungaro-a-serbia.texto: Note delivered in Belgrade by the Austro-Hungarian ambassador Wladimir Giesl on 23 July 1914, almost a month after the Sarajevo assassination, with a 48-hour deadline. It demanded that Serbia condemn anti-Austrian propaganda, dissolve the Narodna Odbrana, dismiss officers and officials named by Vienna, and accept the participation of Austro-Hungarian agents in suppressing the movement and in the investigation of the assassination.

The British foreign secretary Edward Grey called it “the most formidable document ever addressed by one State to another independent State”; many historians argue that it was drafted to be rejected. It is the starting point of the escalation that led to general war.
English translation in the World War I Document Archive (Brigham Young University)
German text in the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/respuesta-serbia-al-ultimatum/ti.texto: Serbian reply to the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum

fuentes/respuesta-serbia-al-ultimatum/re.texto: Reply that Prime Minister Nikola Pašić delivered in person to the Austro-Hungarian ambassador on 25 July 1914, shortly before the deadline expired. It accepted almost all the demands, some with reservations, but rejected the participation of Austro-Hungarian officials in the judicial inquiry inside Serbia and offered to refer the dispute to the tribunal at The Hague.

fuentes/respuesta-serbia-al-ultimatum/po.texto: Vienna deemed it insufficient and broke off relations that same day, although Wilhelm II himself wrote on reading it that it removed every reason for war. It shows the extent to which the rupture was an Austro-Hungarian decision.

fuentes/respuesta-serbia-al-ultimatum/le.texto: English translation at the World War I Document Archive
French original at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-austrohung.texto: Austro-Hungarian declaration of war on Serbia

Telegram sent by Foreign Minister Berchtold to the Serbian government on 28 July 1914, declaring that, since Serbia had not replied satisfactorily to the note of 23 July, Austria-Hungary considered itself in a state of war with it. That same night Austro-Hungarian artillery began shelling Belgrade.
It was the first declaration of war of the First World War and is often remembered as the first sent by telegram. It set in motion the Russian and German mobilizations.
Text at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/a-mis-pueblos/resumen.texto: Manifesto signed by Franz Joseph at Bad Ischl on 28 July 1914 and published the next day in all the languages of the empire. The 83-year-old emperor explained that he had exhausted peaceful means in the face of the “machinations” of an adversary “full of hatred” and called on his peoples to go to war against Serbia.

fuentes/a-mis-pueblos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the public justification of the war addressed to the subjects of a multinational empire that would not survive it.

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-alemana-a-.texto: German declaration of war on Russia

Note delivered in Saint Petersburg to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Sazonov by the German ambassador Friedrich von Pourtalès on 1 August 1914, after Russia failed to answer the German ultimatum demanding that it halt its general mobilization within twelve hours. It declared that Germany considered itself in a state of war with Russia.
It turned the Austro-Serbian war into a war between great powers and triggered the Franco-Russian alliance.
Text at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/ultimatum-aleman-a-belgica/resum.texto: Note delivered in Brussels on the evening of 2 August 1914 which, on the pretext of an alleged French plan to advance along the Meuse, requested free passage for German troops and gave twelve hours to reply; if Belgium resisted, it would be treated as an enemy. The Belgian government rejected it the following morning, invoking its neutrality, guaranteed by the powers in 1839.

fuentes/ultimatum-aleman-a-belgica/por_q.texto: The invasion that followed on 4 August decided the United Kingdom's entry into the war.

fuentes/ultimatum-aleman-a-belgica/leer..texto: The German note at the World War I Document Archive
The Belgian reply at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-alemana-a-.texto: German declaration of war on France

Letter delivered in Paris on 3 August 1914 by Ambassador Wilhelm von Schoen to Prime Minister René Viviani. It justified the war with alleged hostile acts by French aviators, including a bombing of Nuremberg, that never took place.
It shows that the German war plan, which required attacking France first through Belgium, was taking precedence over diplomacy.
Collected Diplomatic Documents Relating to the Outbreak of the European War (1915), Internet Archive

fuentes/discurso-de-grey-1914/titulo.texto: Edward Grey's speech to the House of Commons

fuentes/discurso-de-grey-1914/resumen.texto: Speech of 3 August 1914 in which the Foreign Secretary explained to the House of Commons Britain's commitments to France and its obligation to defend Belgian neutrality, and announced that the United Kingdom could not stand aside. He also reported that Germany had demanded free passage for its troops through Belgium.

fuentes/discurso-de-grey-1914/por_que_im.texto: It swayed Parliament and the Liberal cabinet, until then divided, towards war.

fuentes/discurso-de-grey-1914/leer.0.tit.texto: Verbatim record in the Hansard of the British Parliament

fuentes/discurso-de-grey-1914/leer.1.tit.texto: Text at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/ultimatum-britanico-a-alemania-1.texto: Telegram of 4 August 1914 to the ambassador in Berlin, Edward Goschen, instructing him to demand an assurance that Germany would not violate Belgian neutrality, with a reply due before midnight Berlin time. In their farewell interview, Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg reproached Goschen that the United Kingdom was going to war over “a scrap of paper”, the treaty of 1839.
When it expired unanswered, the United Kingdom and its entire empire were at war with Germany.
Collected Diplomatic Documents Relating to the Outbreak of the European War (1915), with the British Blue Book, Internet Archive

fuentes/telegrama-zimmermann/resumen.texto: Coded telegram of 16 January 1917 to the German ambassador in Mexico, proposing an alliance to the government of Venustiano Carranza should the United States enter the war, with the promise of recovering Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. It was intercepted and deciphered by British naval intelligence, and Wilson made it public on 1 March; Zimmermann admitted it was genuine.

fuentes/telegrama-zimmermann/por_que_imp.texto: Together with unrestricted submarine warfare, it turned American public opinion in favor of entering the war. Mexico rejected the proposal.

fuentes/telegrama-zimmermann/leer.0.titu.texto: German text and translation on Wikisource

fuentes/mensaje-de-guerra-de-wilson/resu.texto: Address to both houses on 2 April 1917 in which Wilson asked for a declaration of war on Germany over unrestricted submarine warfare and the intrigue of the Zimmermann Telegram. He presented the war as a struggle against autocracy and declared that “the world must be made safe for democracy”. Congress voted the declaration on 6 April.

fuentes/mensaje-de-guerra-de-wilson/por_.texto: It took the United States into its first major war in Europe and foreshadowed the program of the Fourteen Points.

fuentes/mensaje-de-guerra-de-wilson/leer.texto: Text at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/decreto-sobre-la-paz/resumen.texto: First decree of the Bolshevik government, adopted by the Second Congress of Soviets on 8 November 1917 (26 October in the Julian calendar). It proposed to all belligerents an immediate peace “without annexations or indemnities”, declared secret diplomacy abolished and announced the publication of the Allies' secret treaties.

fuentes/decreto-sobre-la-paz/por_que_imp.texto: It challenged the warring governments to define their aims, which Wilson did weeks later with the Fourteen Points, and opened the way to the separate peace of Brest-Litovsk.

fuentes/catorce-puntos/resumen.texto: Address to Congress of 8 January 1918 that listed fourteen conditions for peace: open diplomacy, freedom of navigation, free trade, arms reduction, an impartial adjustment of colonial claims, the evacuation of occupied territories, the autonomous development of the peoples of Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, an independent Poland with access to the sea, and a general association of nations.

fuentes/catorce-puntos/por_que_importa.texto: Germany requested the armistice on their basis, and the gap between those promises and the Treaty of Versailles fueled German resentment. The proposal for the League of Nations earned Wilson the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/tratado-de-brest-litovsk/autor.texto: Soviet Russia and the Central Powers

fuentes/tratado-de-brest-litovsk/idioma_.texto: German, Russian, Hungarian, Bulgarian and Ottoman Turkish

fuentes/tratado-de-brest-litovsk/resumen.texto: Peace signed on 3 March 1918 between Bolshevik Russia and Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire, after Trotsky walked out of the negotiations with the formula “neither war nor peace” and Germany resumed its advance. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic countries, Finland and Ukraine, with about a third of its population and much of its industry and coal.

fuentes/tratado-de-brest-litovsk/por_que.texto: It took Russia out of the war and allowed Germany to move troops west for its spring offensive. The armistice of November 1918 annulled it.

fuentes/armisticio-de-compiegne/resumen.texto: Armistice signed at about five in the morning on 11 November 1918 in Marshal Foch's railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, in force from eleven o'clock. Germany was to evacuate France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine, withdraw behind the Rhine, hand over much of its artillery, aircraft and fleet and renounce Brest-Litovsk, while the Allied naval blockade continued.

fuentes/armisticio-de-compiegne/por_que_.texto: It ended the fighting of the First World War. Hitler forced France to sign its 1940 armistice in the same carriage.

fuentes/armisticio-de-compiegne/leer.0.t.texto: Terms of the armistice at the World War I Document Archive

fuentes/tratado-de-versalles/resumen.texto: Peace treaty between the Allies and Germany signed in the Hall of Mirrors on 28 June 1919, exactly five years after the Sarajevo assassination. Its Part I is the Covenant of the League of Nations. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine, territories to Poland and all its colonies, had to demilitarize the Rhineland and limit its army to 100,000 men, and Article 231 held it responsible for the damage of the war as the basis for reparations.

fuentes/tratado-de-versalles/por_que_imp.texto: In Germany it was denounced as a “Diktat”, and its revision was a rallying cry of Nazism. Keynes considered it economically ruinous; other historians argue that it was not as harsh as claimed and that it was above all its enforcement that failed.

fuentes/tratado-de-versalles/leer.1.titu.texto: Text by parts at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/pacto-de-la-sociedad-de-naciones.texto: Covenant of the League of Nations

Founding document of the League of Nations, drafted by a commission chaired by Wilson, approved by the Peace Conference on 28 April 1919 and incorporated as Part I of the peace treaties. It created the Assembly, the Council and the Secretariat, based in Geneva; it committed members to respect one another's territorial integrity (Art. 10), submit their disputes to arbitration and impose sanctions on the aggressor (Art. 16), and established the mandate system over the former German and Ottoman colonies (Art. 22).
It was the first worldwide collective security organization. The United States never joined it and it could not stop the aggressions of the 1930s, but it served as a model for the UN.
Part I of the Treaty of Versailles on Wikisource

fuentes/pacto-briand-kellogg/resumen.texto: Treaty signed in Paris on 27 August 1928 by which the parties condemned recourse to war for the solution of international disputes and renounced it as an instrument of national policy. It grew out of a bilateral Franco-American proposal by Briand that Secretary of State Frank Kellogg turned into a multilateral one; it eventually had more than sixty state parties.

fuentes/pacto-briand-kellogg/por_que_imp.texto: It had no enforcement mechanisms and did not prevent war, but it was the basis of the charge of “crimes against peace” at Nuremberg and Tokyo. Kellogg received the 1929 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/informe-lytton/autor.texto: Lytton Commission of the League of Nations

fuentes/informe-lytton/resumen.texto: Report of the League of Nations commission chaired by Lord Lytton, published in October 1932 after an on-site investigation of the Mukden Incident. It concluded that the Japanese military action had not been self-defense and that the state of Manchukuo was not the product of a genuine independence movement, although it acknowledged Japan's special interests in Manchuria.

fuentes/informe-lytton/por_que_importa.texto: When the Assembly adopted it in February 1933, Japan withdrew from the League of Nations: it was the first major failure of collective security.

fuentes/homenaje-a-cataluna/resumen.texto: George Orwell's account of his experience as a POUM militiaman on the Aragon front, where he was wounded, and of the May Days of 1937 in Barcelona, when the Communists suppressed the anarchists and the POUM. It describes revolutionary Barcelona and criticizes the version of the war spread by the press.

fuentes/homenaje-a-cataluna/por_que_impo.texto: A testimony of the Spanish Civil War from the anti-Stalinist left; it sold poorly at the time and became a classic after its author's death.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-munich/autor.texto: Adolf Hitler, Neville Chamberlain, Édouard Daladier and Benito Mussolini

fuentes/acuerdo-de-munich/resumen.texto: Agreement signed in the early hours of 30 September 1938 by Germany, the United Kingdom, France and Italy, without the participation of Czechoslovakia, which required the latter to hand over the Sudetenland to Germany between 1 and 10 October. Chamberlain returned to London with an Anglo-German declaration signed by Hitler and presented it as “peace for our time”.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-munich/por_que_import.texto: It is the symbol of the policy of appeasement: in March 1939 Hitler occupied the rest of Bohemia and Moravia, and “Munich” became a byword for giving in to an aggressor. Its defenders argue that it bought time for British rearmament.

fuentes/pacto-ribbentrop-molotov/autor.texto: Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov

fuentes/pacto-ribbentrop-molotov/resumen.texto: Non-aggression treaty signed in Moscow on the night of 23 August 1939 by the foreign ministers of Germany and the USSR, in the presence of Stalin. A secret additional protocol divided Eastern Europe into spheres of influence: western Poland for Germany; eastern Poland, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia for the USSR, to which Lithuania was added in September.

fuentes/pacto-ribbentrop-molotov/por_que.texto: It gave Hitler a free hand to invade Poland a week later. The USSR denied the existence of the secret protocol until 1989.

fuentes/pacto-ribbentrop-molotov/leer.0..texto: Non-aggression treaty at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/pacto-ribbentrop-molotov/leer.1..texto: Secret additional protocol at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/ultimatum-britanico-1939/resumen.texto: Note that Ambassador Nevile Henderson delivered in Berlin at nine in the morning on 3 September 1939, with a deadline of eleven o'clock, demanding an assurance that Germany would halt its attack on Poland and withdraw its troops. France delivered a similar note that expired at five in the afternoon.

fuentes/ultimatum-britanico-1939/por_que.texto: It fulfilled the British guarantee to Poland of March 1939 and opened the war in the west, although for months there was hardly any fighting there.

fuentes/ultimatum-britanico-1939/leer.0..texto: Halifax's instructions to Henderson with the text of the ultimatum (British Blue Book, No. 118), at the Avalon Project

fuentes/discurso-de-chamberlain-1939/res.texto: BBC broadcast at 11:15 on 3 September 1939, from 10 Downing Street, in which Chamberlain announced that no reply to the ultimatum had been received and that “consequently this country is at war with Germany”. He acknowledged the failure of his long struggle for peace and blamed Hitler.

fuentes/discurso-de-chamberlain-1939/por.texto: It is the announcement of Britain's entry into the Second World War.

fuentes/sangre-esfuerzo-lagrimas-y-sudor.texto: Churchill's first speech as prime minister to the House of Commons, on 13 May 1940, three days after he took office and the German offensive in the west began. He said he had nothing to offer but “blood, toil, tears and sweat” and summed up his aim in one word: “victory”.
It set the tone of British resistance at the worst moment of the war.

fuentes/lucharemos-en-las-playas/titulo.texto: We Shall Fight on the Beaches

fuentes/lucharemos-en-las-playas/resumen.texto: Speech to the Commons of 4 June 1940, at the end of the Dunkirk evacuation. He celebrated the rescue but warned that “wars are not won by evacuations”, and pledged that the United Kingdom would fight on the beaches, in the fields, in the streets and in the hills and that it would “never surrender”.

fuentes/lucharemos-en-las-playas/por_que.texto: It implicitly rejected any negotiation with Hitler, which part of the cabinet was considering.

fuentes/su-hora-mas-gloriosa/resumen.texto: Speech of 18 June 1940, as France was seeking an armistice. Churchill announced that the Battle of France was over and the Battle of Britain was about to begin, and called for conduct such that, a thousand years from now, people would say: “this was their finest hour”.

fuentes/su-hora-mas-gloriosa/por_que_imp.texto: It prepared the British to stand alone against Germany.

fuentes/llamamiento-del-18-de-junio/resu.texto: BBC broadcast of 18 June 1940 in which De Gaulle, then a little-known general, rejected Marshal Pétain's request for an armistice and called on the French in British territory to join him in continuing the fight: “the flame of French resistance must not and shall not go out”. Few heard it and it was not recorded.

fuentes/llamamiento-del-18-de-junio/por_.texto: It is regarded as the founding act of Free France and of the Resistance.

fuentes/llamamiento-del-18-de-junio/leer.texto: Text of the appeal (Presidency of the French Republic)

fuentes/cuatro-libertades/resumen.texto: Annual message to Congress of 6 January 1941, while the United States was still neutral, in which Roosevelt called for aid to the democracies at war and proposed a world founded on four essential freedoms: freedom of speech and expression, freedom of worship, freedom from want and freedom from fear.

fuentes/cuatro-libertades/por_que_import.texto: It anticipated the Lend-Lease Act and the Atlantic Charter, and its language passed into the preamble of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

fuentes/carta-del-atlantico/autor.texto: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill

fuentes/carta-del-atlantico/resumen.texto: Joint declaration of 14 August 1941, agreed by Roosevelt and Churchill aboard warships in Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, when the United States was not yet at war. In eight points it rejected territorial aggrandizement and affirmed the right of peoples to choose their form of government, equal access to trade, freedom of the seas and the disarmament of aggressors, and announced a system of general security.

fuentes/carta-del-atlantico/por_que_impo.texto: It was the basis of the Declaration by United Nations of 1942 and of the UN Charter. Anti-colonial movements invoked its point on self-determination, which Churchill understood as limited to occupied Europe.

fuentes/discurso-de-la-infamia/resumen.texto: Speech of about seven minutes to Congress on 8 December 1941, the day after the attack on Pearl Harbor, which begins by calling 7 December “a date which will live in infamy”. It listed the Japanese attacks in the Pacific during those hours and asked that a state of war with Japan be declared.

fuentes/discurso-de-la-infamia/por_que_i.texto: Less than an hour later Congress approved the declaration of war with a single vote against, that of the pacifist Jeannette Rankin.

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-a-japon/ti.texto: United States declaration of war on Japan

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-a-japon/re.texto: Joint resolution passed on 8 December 1941 by 82 votes to 0 in the Senate and 388 to 1 in the House of Representatives, formally declaring a state of war with the Empire of Japan, which it said had been thrust upon the country by its “unprovoked acts” of war. Roosevelt signed it that same afternoon.

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-a-japon/po.texto: Together with those voted on 11 December against Germany and Italy and in June 1942 against Bulgaria, Hungary and Romania, they are the last formal declarations of war by the United States: later wars were fought under congressional authorizations or UN resolutions.

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-a-japon/le.texto: Joint resolution of 1941, Statutes at Large (55 Stat. 795)

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-alemana-a-.texto: German declaration of war on the United States

Note that Ribbentrop handed to the American chargé d'affaires in Berlin on 11 December 1941, while Hitler announced the war in the Reichstag; Italy did the same that day. It accused Roosevelt of violating neutrality with attacks on German ships. The Tripartite Pact, being defensive, did not oblige Germany to take that step.
Many historians consider it one of Hitler's greatest strategic blunders: it allowed Roosevelt to turn the American effort towards Europe.

fuentes/declaracion-de-las-naciones-unid.texto: Declaration signed in Washington on 1 January 1942 by twenty-six governments at war with the Axis, led by the United States, the United Kingdom, the USSR and China. They subscribed to the principles of the Atlantic Charter and pledged to employ all their resources in the war and not to make a separate peace.
It was the first official use of the term “United Nations”, proposed by Roosevelt, and the nucleus of the future organization.

fuentes/protocolo-de-wannsee/resumen.texto: Minutes of the meeting of 20 January 1942 in a villa on the shore of Lake Wannsee, in Berlin, where fifteen senior officials of the state, the party and the SS, convened by Heydrich, coordinated the “final solution of the Jewish question”. Drafted by Eichmann in euphemistic language, it put at eleven million the number of Jews in Europe who were to be “evacuated to the east” and anticipated that many would die from forced labor. Of the thirty copies only one survived, found in 1947.

fuentes/protocolo-de-wannsee/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most frequently cited documentary evidence of the bureaucratic coordination of the Holocaust and was used in the postwar trials.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-yalta/autor.texto: Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin

fuentes/acuerdos-de-yalta/resumen.texto: Protocol and communiqué of the Crimea Conference, held from 4 to 11 February 1945. They agreed on dividing Germany into occupation zones, including one for France; the “Declaration on Liberated Europe”, which promised free elections; an enlarged Polish government and Poland's eastern border on the Curzon Line; the summoning of the San Francisco Conference; and, in a secret agreement, the USSR's entry into the war against Japan in exchange for southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-yalta/por_que_import.texto: In the West it was criticized as the handing over of Eastern Europe to Stalin; its defenders reply that the Red Army already occupied the region and that the promises of free elections went unfulfilled because of Soviet decisions.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-yalta/leer.0.titulo.texto: Protocol and agreements at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/declaracion-de-potsdam/autor.texto: Harry S. Truman, Winston Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek

fuentes/declaracion-de-potsdam/resumen.texto: Ultimatum to Japan issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, the United Kingdom and China. In thirteen points it demanded the unconditional surrender of the Japanese armed forces, the elimination of those who had led the country into conquest, occupation, the punishment of war criminals and the reduction of Japanese territory to the main islands; the alternative was “prompt and utter destruction”. It mentioned neither the atomic bomb nor the future of the emperor.

fuentes/declaracion-de-potsdam/por_que_i.texto: The Japanese government announced that it would disregard it; ten days later the bomb fell on Hiroshima, and on 14 August Japan accepted it.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-potsdam/autor.texto: Harry S. Truman, Joseph Stalin and Clement Attlee

fuentes/acuerdo-de-potsdam/resumen.texto: Communiqué of the Potsdam Conference (17 July to 2 August 1945). It set out the principles for the occupation of Germany —demilitarization, denazification, democratization and decentralization—, reparations, Polish administration of the territories east of the Oder–Neisse line and the “orderly and humane” transfer of German populations from Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-potsdam/por_que_impor.texto: It laid the foundations for the division of Germany and provided cover for the expulsion of millions of Germans from Eastern Europe.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-potsdam/leer.1.titulo.texto: Protocol of the conference at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/acta-de-rendicion-alemana/resume.texto: Unconditional surrender of all German armed forces, signed by General Jodl at Eisenhower's headquarters in Reims on 7 May 1945 and ratified, at Soviet request, by Field Marshal Keitel in Berlin-Karlshorst on the night of 8 May. It took effect at 23:01 Central European Time on 8 May, when it was already the 9th in Moscow.

fuentes/acta-de-rendicion-alemana/por_qu.texto: It ended the war in Europe; because of the time difference, the West celebrates victory on 8 May and Russia on 9 May.

fuentes/acta-de-rendicion-alemana/leer.0.texto: Reims and Berlin texts on Wikisource

fuentes/declaracion-de-truman-sobre-hiro.texto: Truman's statement on the Hiroshima bomb

Statement released in Washington on 6 August 1945, some sixteen hours after the bombing, revealing that an atomic bomb, “a harnessing of the basic power of the universe”, had been dropped on Hiroshima. It threatened Japan with “a rain of ruin from the air, the like of which has never been seen” if it did not accept the Potsdam terms, and promised to study the use of atomic energy for peace.
It is the first public announcement of the existence of nuclear weapons.
Text at the Truman Presidential Library

fuentes/discurso-de-rendicion-de-hirohit.texto: Imperial Rescript on the Termination of the War

Message recorded on the night of 14 August 1945 and broadcast by radio at noon on the 15th, the first time the Japanese people heard their emperor's voice. In courtly Japanese and without using the word “surrender”, it announced the acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration, alluded to “a new and most cruel bomb” and called on the people to “endure the unendurable”. The night before, a group of officers attempted a coup to prevent the broadcast.
It ended the Pacific War and showed the authority the emperor still held over the military.

fuentes/acta-de-rendicion-de-japon/resum.texto: Signed aboard the American battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945 by Foreign Minister Shigemitsu, on behalf of the emperor and the government, and General Umezu, for the Imperial General Headquarters; MacArthur accepted it as Supreme Allied Commander, together with representatives of eight other countries. Japan accepted the Potsdam Declaration and the unconditional surrender of all its forces, and the emperor's authority was made subject to the Supreme Commander.

fuentes/acta-de-rendicion-de-japon/por_q.texto: It marks the official end of the Second World War.

fuentes/estatuto-de-londres/titulo.texto: Charter of the International Military Tribunal

fuentes/estatuto-de-londres/autor.texto: The United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Soviet Union

fuentes/estatuto-de-londres/resumen.texto: Annex to the London Agreement of 8 August 1945 that created the tribunal to try the major war criminals of the European Axis. It defined three categories of offences —crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity—, established the individual responsibility of heads of state and officials, and denied that obeying superior orders freed a defendant from guilt.

fuentes/estatuto-de-londres/por_que_impo.texto: Legal basis of the Nuremberg trial and of later international criminal law. Its critics denounced it as “victors' justice” that retroactively applied new offences.

fuentes/sentencia-de-nuremberg/titulo.texto: Judgment of the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg

fuentes/sentencia-de-nuremberg/resumen.texto: Judgment read on 30 September and 1 October 1946 against twenty-two Nazi leaders, one of whom, Martin Bormann, was tried in absentia. It sentenced twelve to death and seven to prison, acquitted three (Hjalmar Schacht, Franz von Papen and Hans Fritzsche), and declared the Nazi Party leadership, the SS, the SD and the Gestapo criminal organizations. Göring committed suicide before his execution, and ten others were hanged on 16 October.

fuentes/sentencia-de-nuremberg/por_que_i.texto: First judgment by an international tribunal against the leaders of a state; it documented the Holocaust and the war of aggression using Germany's own evidence. The UN adopted its principles in 1946.

fuentes/sentencia-de-nuremberg/leer.0.ti.texto: Full judgment, by chapter, at the Avalon Project (Yale)

fuentes/eichmann-en-jerusalen/resumen.texto: Hannah Arendt's report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, first published in The New Yorker and as a book in 1963. It argues that Eichmann was not a fanatical monster but an obedient and “terribly normal” functionary, and coins the phrase “the banality of evil”; it also criticizes the cooperation of some Jewish councils with the Nazis.

fuentes/eichmann-en-jerusalen/por_que_im.texto: It sparked a lasting controversy; later research, such as that of Bettina Stangneth, showed an Eichmann more ideologically committed than Arendt believed.

fuentes/carta-de-la-onu/idioma_original.texto: Chinese, French, Russian, English and Spanish

fuentes/carta-de-la-onu/resumen.texto: Founding treaty of the United Nations, signed on 26 June 1945 by fifty states at the San Francisco Conference and in force since 24 October. It prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state (art. 2.4), except in self-defence (art. 51) or with the authorization of the Security Council (Chapter VII), in which five permanent members hold a veto. It also creates the General Assembly, the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat.

fuentes/carta-de-la-onu/por_que_importa.texto: It has been the central norm of the international order since 1945. The UN and its Secretary-General Kofi Annan were awarded the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/carta-de-la-onu/leer.0.titulo.texto: Official Spanish text on the UN website

fuentes/carta-de-la-onu/leer.1.titulo.texto: Official English text on the UN website

fuentes/declaracion-universal-de-derecho.texto: Adopted by the General Assembly on 10 December 1948 at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris (Resolution 217 A), with 48 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions: the Soviet bloc, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. In thirty articles it sets out civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. It was drafted by a commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, with René Cassin, Peng Chun Chang, Charles Malik and John Humphrey among its drafters.
It is not a binding treaty, but it inspired the international covenants of 1966 and dozens of constitutions. Cassin was awarded the 1968 Nobel Peace Prize.
Official Spanish text on the UN website

fuentes/convencion-sobre-el-genocidio/ti.texto: Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide

fuentes/convencion-sobre-el-genocidio/id.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian and Chinese

fuentes/convencion-sobre-el-genocidio/re.texto: Adopted by the General Assembly on 9 December 1948, one day before the Universal Declaration, and in force since 1951. It defines genocide as certain acts committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group” and obliges states to prevent and punish it. It was promoted by Raphael Lemkin, who had coined the word in 1944.

fuentes/convencion-sobre-el-genocidio/po.texto: First human rights treaty of the UN. It was applied by the tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia and is the basis for cases before the International Court of Justice such as Bosnia v. Serbia, The Gambia v. Myanmar, Ukraine v. Russia and South Africa v. Israel.

fuentes/convencion-sobre-el-genocidio/le.texto: Resolution 260 (III) with the text of the convention, in the UN document system

fuentes/convenios-de-ginebra/resumen.texto: Four conventions signed on 12 August 1949 that protect wounded and sick soldiers in the field, the shipwrecked, prisoners of war and, as a new development after the Second World War, civilians in enemy hands or in occupied territory. Their Common Article 3 also applies to internal wars. They update earlier conventions dating back to 1864 and are supplemented by protocols of 1977 and 2005.

fuentes/convenios-de-ginebra/por_que_imp.texto: Ratified by every state in the world, they are the core of international humanitarian law. Their custodian, the International Committee of the Red Cross, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917, 1944 and 1963.

fuentes/convenios-de-ginebra/leer.0.titu.texto: Fourth Convention and links to the other three in the ICRC treaty database

fuentes/telegrama-largo/resumen.texto: Cable of some five thousand words sent from the Moscow embassy to the State Department on 22 February 1946. It explained Soviet hostility by traditional Russian insecurity and by Marxist-Leninist ideology, and argued that the USSR would not risk confrontation with a determined force and could be contained without war. Kennan expanded it in the article “The Sources of Soviet Conduct”, signed “X”, in 1947.

fuentes/telegrama-largo/por_que_importa.texto: It was the intellectual foundation of the containment policy the United States pursued during the Cold War.

fuentes/discurso-del-telon-de-acero/titu.texto: The Sinews of Peace (Iron Curtain speech)

fuentes/discurso-del-telon-de-acero/resu.texto: Lecture given by Churchill, by then out of office, on 5 March 1946 at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with Truman in attendance. He stated that “from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent”, behind which the communist parties were seizing control, and proposed a “special relationship” between the British and the Americans.

fuentes/discurso-del-telon-de-acero/por_.texto: It popularized the image that would give its name to the division of Europe; Stalin responded by comparing Churchill to Hitler.

fuentes/discurso-del-telon-de-acero/leer.texto: Text on the International Churchill Society website

fuentes/doctrina-truman/resumen.texto: Speech to Congress on 12 March 1947 in which Truman requested 400 million dollars for Greece, engaged in a civil war with the communists, and Turkey, under pressure from the USSR. He stated that the policy of the United States must be “to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures”.

fuentes/doctrina-truman/por_que_importa.texto: It is regarded as the formal beginning of the Cold War and of the policy of containment.

fuentes/plan-marshall/resumen.texto: Speech by the Secretary of State at the Harvard commencement of 5 June 1947, offering American aid for the reconstruction of Europe if the Europeans themselves agreed on a joint programme. It took shape in the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948, which by 1952 had transferred more than 13 billion dollars to Western Europe; the USSR rejected it and made Poland and Czechoslovakia reject it as well.

fuentes/plan-marshall/por_que_importa.texto: It accelerated the recovery of Western Europe, tied it to the United States and deepened the division of the continent. Marshall was awarded the 1953 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/tratado-del-atlantico-norte/resu.texto: Treaty signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve states of Western Europe and North America. Its Article 5 states that an armed attack against one of them shall be considered an attack against all; it has been invoked only once, after the attacks of 11 September 2001. The alliance reached thirty-two members with the accession of Finland in 2023 and Sweden in 2024.

fuentes/tratado-del-atlantico-norte/por_.texto: It is the longest-lasting military alliance of the contemporary era. Its eastward expansion after 1991 is one of Russia's central arguments against the West.

fuentes/declaracion-schuman/resumen.texto: Declaration read on 9 May 1950 by the French Foreign Minister, prepared by Jean Monnet, proposing to place Franco-German coal and steel production under a common High Authority open to other countries. In this way, a war between France and Germany would become “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible”.

fuentes/declaracion-schuman/por_que_impo.texto: It gave rise to the European Coal and Steel Community (1951), the first step in European integration; 9 May is Europe Day.

fuentes/declaracion-schuman/leer.0.titul.texto: Text on the European Union website

fuentes/pacto-de-varsovia/autor.texto: The Soviet Union and seven Eastern European states

fuentes/pacto-de-varsovia/resumen.texto: Treaty signed in Warsaw on 14 May 1955 by the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania and the German Democratic Republic, days after West Germany joined NATO. It created a unified military command under Soviet leadership.

fuentes/pacto-de-varsovia/por_que_import.texto: It was NATO's counterweight during the Cold War; its troops never fought the West, but instead invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968. It was dissolved in 1991.

fuentes/tratado-de-roma/autor.texto: Six founding states of the EEC

fuentes/tratado-de-roma/resumen.texto: Signed in Rome on 25 March 1957 by France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, it created the European Economic Community, with a common market and a customs union; a parallel treaty created Euratom. It established the Commission, the Council, the Parliamentary Assembly and the Court of Justice.

fuentes/tratado-de-roma/por_que_importa.texto: It is the basis of today's European Union; in amended form, it remains in force as the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. The Union was awarded the 2012 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/ley-de-independencia-de-la-india.texto: Act of the British Parliament passed on 18 July 1947 that created, from 15 August, two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, following the plan announced by Viceroy Mountbatten on 3 June. The partition boundaries in Punjab and Bengal were drawn by a commission chaired by Cyril Radcliffe and were not published until 17 August.
It ended British rule in the subcontinent and gave legal form to partition, one of the largest forced migrations in history.

fuentes/cita-con-el-destino/resumen.texto: Speech delivered by Nehru to the Constituent Assembly close to midnight on 14–15 August 1947: “At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.” He remembered Gandhi and those suffering the violence of partition.

fuentes/cita-con-el-destino/por_que_impo.texto: It is the founding speech of independent India and one of the great texts of decolonization.

fuentes/resolucion-1514/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian and Chinese

fuentes/resolucion-1514/resumen.texto: Declaration adopted on 14 December 1960 by 89 votes in favour, none against and nine abstentions, including those of the main colonial powers. It proclaims that the subjection of peoples to alien domination denies fundamental human rights, that all peoples have the right to self-determination and that lack of preparedness should never serve as a pretext for delaying independence; it also protects the territorial integrity of countries.

fuentes/resolucion-1514/por_que_importa.texto: It was adopted in the “Year of Africa”, when seventeen of the continent's colonies became independent, and it is the basis of the UN Special Committee on Decolonization.

fuentes/resolucion-1514/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/titu.texto: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/auto.texto: The United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/idio.texto: English, Russian, French, Spanish and Chinese

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/resu.texto: Opened for signature on 1 July 1968 in Washington, London and Moscow and in force since 1970. It distinguishes between the states that had tested nuclear weapons before 1967, which undertake not to transfer them and to negotiate disarmament (art. VI), and all others, which renounce acquiring them in exchange for access to peaceful nuclear energy under inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency. In 1995 it was extended indefinitely.

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/por_.texto: It is the arms control treaty with the most parties. India, Pakistan and Israel never signed it, and North Korea withdrew in 2003. The ICAN campaign, which promoted a treaty for a total ban, was awarded the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/tratado-de-no-proliferacion/leer.texto: General Assembly Resolution 2373 with the treaty annexed

fuentes/acta-final-de-helsinki/autor.texto: Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe

fuentes/acta-final-de-helsinki/idioma_or.texto: English, French, German, Italian, Russian and Spanish

fuentes/acta-final-de-helsinki/resumen.texto: Signed on 1 August 1975 by thirty-five states: all European states except Albania, plus the United States and Canada. It recognized the inviolability of post-war borders and non-intervention in internal affairs, which the USSR sought, and included respect for human rights and the free movement of people and ideas, which the West sought.

fuentes/acta-final-de-helsinki/por_que_i.texto: Dissidents such as the Czechoslovak Charter 77 and the Helsinki groups in the USSR invoked its human rights commitments; it gave rise to today's OSCE.

fuentes/tratado-de-maastricht/autor.texto: Twelve states of the European Communities

fuentes/tratado-de-maastricht/idioma_ori.texto: The nine official languages of the Communities

fuentes/tratado-de-maastricht/resumen.texto: Treaty on European Union, signed in Maastricht on 7 February 1992 by the twelve members of the European Communities and in force since November 1993. It created the European Union on three “pillars” —the communities, the common foreign and security policy, and cooperation in justice and home affairs—, European citizenship and the path toward monetary union and the euro, with fiscal convergence criteria.

fuentes/tratado-de-maastricht/por_que_im.texto: It transformed an economic community into a political union. Denmark rejected it in its first referendum and France approved it by a narrow margin.

fuentes/estatuto-de-roma/titulo.texto: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court

fuentes/estatuto-de-roma/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/estatuto-de-roma/resumen.texto: Treaty adopted in Rome on 17 July 1998 by 120 votes in favour and seven against, including the United States, China and Israel. It created the International Criminal Court, based in The Hague, with jurisdiction to try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and, since 2018, the crime of aggression, when states are unable or unwilling to do so. It entered into force on 1 July 2002.

fuentes/estatuto-de-roma/por_que_importa.texto: First permanent international criminal court. The United States, Russia, China and India are not parties, and its warrants against Vladimir Putin (2023) and Benjamin Netanyahu (2024) showed the limits of its ability to enforce them.

fuentes/estatuto-de-roma/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text on the International Criminal Court website

fuentes/protocolo-de-kioto/autor.texto: Conference of the Parties to the Framework Convention on Climate Change

fuentes/protocolo-de-kioto/idioma_origin.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/protocolo-de-kioto/resumen.texto: Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in Kyoto on 11 December 1997 and in force since 2005. It required industrialized countries to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions by an average of 5% below 1990 levels between 2008 and 2012; developing countries had no targets, and the United States never ratified it.

fuentes/protocolo-de-kioto/por_que_impor.texto: First agreement with binding emissions targets. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and Al Gore were awarded the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/protocolo-de-kioto/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text on the Framework Convention on Climate Change website

fuentes/acuerdo-de-paris/autor.texto: Conference of the Parties to the Framework Convention on Climate Change

fuentes/acuerdo-de-paris/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/acuerdo-de-paris/resumen.texto: Adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 and in force since November 2016. It sets the goal of holding the increase in global average temperature to “well below” 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C, through contributions that each country sets and reviews every five years.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-paris/por_que_importa.texto: It brings together almost every country in the world, but its targets are not binding. The United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-paris/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text on the Framework Convention on Climate Change website

fuentes/resolucion-83/resumen.texto: Resolution of 27 June 1950, two days after the North Korean invasion of the South, which recommended that UN members furnish the Republic of Korea with the assistance needed to repel the attack and restore peace. It could be adopted because the USSR had been boycotting the Council since January, in protest at China's seat being held by the Nationalist government in Taiwan.

fuentes/resolucion-83/por_que_importa.texto: The first time the UN authorized collective military action; Resolution 84 placed those forces under a unified US command.

fuentes/resolucion-83/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/armisticio-de-corea/autor.texto: United Nations Command, Korean People's Army and Chinese People's Volunteers

fuentes/armisticio-de-corea/resumen.texto: Signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 by US General William Harrison, for the United Nations Command, and North Korean General Nam Il; South Korea did not sign it. It established a ceasefire, a demarcation line near the 38th parallel with a demilitarized zone four kilometers wide, and the exchange of prisoners.

fuentes/armisticio-de-corea/por_que_impo.texto: No peace treaty was ever signed: the two Koreas remain technically at war, and the demilitarized zone is one of the most heavily guarded borders in the world.

fuentes/declaracion-de-independencia-de-.texto: Proclamation of Independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam

Proclamation read by Ho Chi Minh in Ba Dinh Square in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, the same day as the Japanese surrender. It opens by quoting the United States Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, lists the abuses of French colonialism and founds the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.
France did not recognize it, and at the end of 1946 the Indochina War began, the prelude to the Vietnam War.

fuentes/discurso-secreto/titulo.texto: On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences

fuentes/discurso-secreto/resumen.texto: Report that Khrushchev read at a closed session of the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union on 25 February 1956. He denounced Stalin's purges, torture, deportations of entire peoples and military mistakes, though he did not question collectivization or Leninism. It was leaked to the West, and The New York Times published it in June.

fuentes/discurso-secreto/por_que_importa.texto: It opened the “Thaw” in the USSR and shook world communism; it contributed to the uprisings in Poland and Hungary that year.

fuentes/discurso-de-despedida-de-eisenho.texto: Televised address of 17 January 1961, three days before he left the presidency. Eisenhower warned that the conjunction of a permanent arms industry and a large military establishment was new in the American experience and called for guarding against the “unwarranted influence” of the “military-industrial complex”.
That the warning came from a general who had commanded the largest invasion in history gave it an authority the expression still carries.

fuentes/discurso-de-kennedy-sobre-cuba/t.texto: Kennedy's address on the missiles in Cuba

fuentes/discurso-de-kennedy-sobre-cuba/r.texto: Televised address of 22 October 1962 in which Kennedy revealed that spy planes had photographed Soviet missile bases under construction in Cuba. He announced a naval “quarantine” on shipments of offensive weapons to the island and warned that any missile launched from Cuba would be treated as a Soviet attack on the United States.

fuentes/discurso-de-kennedy-sobre-cuba/p.texto: It made the Cuban Missile Crisis public and set the US position for the days that followed.

fuentes/ich-bin-ein-berliner/resumen.texto: Speech by Kennedy before hundreds of thousands of people in front of the Schöneberg city hall in West Berlin on 26 June 1963, almost two years after the Wall was built. He declared that all free men are citizens of Berlin and that he therefore took pride in saying “Ich bin ein Berliner” (“I am a Berliner”).

fuentes/ich-bin-ein-berliner/por_que_imp.texto: A symbol of the American commitment to West Berlin. The story that the phrase means “I am a jelly doughnut” is a myth: it is correct German.

fuentes/resolucion-de-tonkin/resumen.texto: Joint resolution passed on 7 August 1964, unanimously in the House of Representatives and by 88 votes to 2 in the Senate, after reported North Vietnamese attacks on US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin. It authorized the president to take “all necessary measures” to repel attacks against US forces and to prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia, without declaring war.

fuentes/resolucion-de-tonkin/por_que_imp.texto: Johnson used it as the legal basis for escalation in Vietnam; it later emerged that the second attack, on 4 August, had not taken place. Congress repealed it in 1971.

fuentes/papeles-del-pentagono/resumen.texto: Secret Department of Defense study of US involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1967, commissioned by Secretary Robert McNamara. Daniel Ellsberg, one of its analysts, leaked it to The New York Times, which began publishing it on 13 June 1971; it showed that successive administrations had expanded the war while saying the opposite.

fuentes/papeles-del-pentagono/por_que_im.texto: The Supreme Court rejected the government's attempt to block its publication, a landmark precedent for press freedom. It was declassified in full in 2011.

fuentes/papeles-del-pentagono/leer.0.tit.texto: The 47 declassified volumes at the U.S. National Archives

fuentes/acuerdos-de-paz-de-paris/autor.texto: United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government

fuentes/acuerdos-de-paz-de-paris/resumen.texto: Agreement signed in Paris on 27 January 1973 that established a ceasefire, the withdrawal of US troops within sixty days and the exchange of prisoners, and left North Vietnamese forces in the South. Its negotiators, Henry Kissinger and Le Duc Tho, were awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize, which Le Duc Tho declined.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-paz-de-paris/por_que.texto: It took the United States out of the war, but fighting between Vietnamese continued and Saigon fell in April 1975.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-evian/autor.texto: French government and Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic

fuentes/acuerdos-de-evian/resumen.texto: Accords signed at Évian-les-Bains on 18 March 1962 between France and the Algerian National Liberation Front. They established a ceasefire from the following day and a self-determination referendum, with guarantees for the Europeans of Algeria and French military bases for a limited period.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-evian/por_que_import.texto: Approved by referendums in France and Algeria, they paved the way for Algerian independence on 5 July 1962. The OAS responded with bombings, and nearly a million Europeans of Algeria left the country.

fuentes/dos-mil-palabras/resumen.texto: Manifesto written by the writer Ludvík Vaculík and signed by dozens of intellectuals, scientists and athletes, published on 27 June 1968 in several Prague newspapers. It called for deepening the Prague Spring reforms from below and warned that the people would defend the reformist government against foreign intervention.

fuentes/dos-mil-palabras/por_que_importa.texto: Moscow cited it as evidence of a “counter-revolution” to justify the August invasion.

fuentes/derriben-este-muro/resumen.texto: Speech by Reagan in front of the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on 12 June 1987, for the city's 750th anniversary. He addressed the Soviet leader: “Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate. Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.”

fuentes/derriben-este-muro/por_que_impor.texto: It drew little attention at the time and became famous after the fall of the Wall in 1989; historians debate how much it contributed to it.

fuentes/tratado-inf/resumen.texto: Treaty signed at the White House on 8 December 1987 that eliminated all ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers. By 1991, 2,692 missiles had been destroyed, with mutual on-site inspections.

fuentes/tratado-inf/por_que_importa.texto: It was the first treaty to eliminate an entire category of nuclear weapons. The United States withdrew in 2019, accusing Russia of violating it, a charge Russia denied. Gorbachev received the 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.

fuentes/tratado-inf/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the State Department archive

fuentes/resolucion-678/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-678/resumen.texto: Resolution of 29 November 1990 that gave Iraq until 15 January 1991 to withdraw from Kuwait, invaded in August, and authorized member states to use “all necessary means” to enforce the previous resolutions. It passed with twelve votes, with Cuba and Yemen against and China abstaining.

fuentes/resolucion-678/por_que_importa.texto: It was the legal basis for Operation Desert Storm and the model for the Council's authorizations of force after the Cold War.

fuentes/resolucion-678/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/memorandum-de-budapest/autor.texto: United States, United Kingdom, Russia and Ukraine

fuentes/memorandum-de-budapest/resumen.texto: Memorandum signed at the CSCE summit in Budapest on 5 December 1994, when Ukraine acceded to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and agreed to hand over to Russia the Soviet nuclear arsenal remaining on its territory. In return, the United States, the United Kingdom and Russia committed to respect its independence, sovereignty and borders and to refrain from the threat or use of force against it. Belarus and Kazakhstan received similar assurances.

fuentes/memorandum-de-budapest/por_que_i.texto: Ukraine and Western governments maintain that Russia violated it in 2014 and 2022; Russia replies that it was not binding with respect to the government that emerged in 2014 from what it considers a coup. It is central to the debate over security guarantees for Ukraine.

fuentes/memorandum-de-budapest/leer.0.ti.texto: UN document A/49/765 containing the memorandum

fuentes/fax-del-genocidio/resumen.texto: Cable of 11 January 1994 in which Canadian General Roméo Dallaire, commander of the UN peacekeeping mission in Rwanda, informed headquarters in New York that an informant from the Hutu regime had revealed arms caches and plans to exterminate the Tutsi. He requested authorization to raid the caches; the Department of Peacekeeping Operations refused and ordered him to inform the Rwandan president.

fuentes/fax-del-genocidio/por_que_import.texto: It is the most frequently cited evidence that the UN had warning of the genocide that began three months later.

fuentes/fax-del-genocidio/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the cable on the Frontline (PBS) website

fuentes/acuerdos-de-dayton/autor.texto: Alija Izetbegović, Franjo Tuđman and Slobodan Milošević

fuentes/acuerdos-de-dayton/resumen.texto: Framework agreement negotiated at an air base in Dayton, Ohio, initialed on 21 November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December by the presidents of Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia. It ended the Bosnian War and divided the country into two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, with a tripartite presidency, an international High Representative and a NATO peacekeeping force.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-dayton/por_que_impor.texto: It stopped the war but entrenched ethnic division; its Annex 4 remains the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

fuentes/aumf-2001/titulo.texto: 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force

fuentes/aumf-2001/resumen.texto: Joint resolution passed on 14 September 2001 and signed by George W. Bush on the 18th, which authorizes the president to use “all necessary and appropriate force” against those nations, organizations or persons he determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the attacks of 11 September, or harbored them. In Congress, only Representative Barbara Lee voted against it.

fuentes/aumf-2001/por_que_importa.texto: It remains in force, and successive administrations have invoked it for operations in more than a dozen countries, far beyond Afghanistan, which its critics call a forever war.

fuentes/informe-de-la-comision-del-11-s/.texto: National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States

Final report of the bipartisan commission chaired by Thomas Kean, published on 22 July 2004. It reconstructs al-Qaeda's planning of the attacks and concludes that the intelligence agencies did not share information and that there was a “failure of imagination” in the face of the threat; it recommended creating a director of national intelligence.
It is the most complete official account of 11 September; it found no operational collaboration between al-Qaeda and Iraq, one of the arguments for the 2003 invasion.
Full report in the commission's archive (University of North Texas Libraries)

fuentes/resolucion-1441/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-1441/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted unanimously on 8 November 2002 that declared Iraq in “material breach” of its disarmament obligations, offered it “a final opportunity” under an enhanced inspection regime and reminded it that it would face “serious consequences” if it did not comply.

fuentes/resolucion-1441/por_que_importa.texto: The United States and the United Kingdom argued that it was sufficient to invade Iraq; France, Russia, Germany and most international lawyers, that a second resolution was needed, which was never put to a vote.

fuentes/resolucion-1441/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/discurso-de-powell-en-la-onu/tit.texto: Colin Powell's presentation to the Security Council

fuentes/discurso-de-powell-en-la-onu/res.texto: Presentation by the US Secretary of State to the Security Council on 5 February 2003, with satellite photos, recordings and testimony offered as proof that Iraq was hiding chemical and biological weapons, mobile laboratories and links to al-Qaeda.

fuentes/discurso-de-powell-en-la-onu/por.texto: The evidence proved false or mistaken: the source on the mobile laboratories, nicknamed “Curveball”, had lied, and Powell later called his speech a “blot” on his career.

fuentes/ultimatum-de-bush-a-sadam/resume.texto: Televised address of 17 March 2003 in which Bush gave Saddam Hussein and his sons 48 hours to leave Iraq, under threat of military conflict commenced “at a time of our choosing”. He argued that the Security Council had not lived up to its responsibilities and that the United States would act on its own authority.

fuentes/ultimatum-de-bush-a-sadam/por_qu.texto: It was the last step before the invasion, which began on 20 March without a new Security Council resolution.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-doha/autor.texto: United States and the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (Taliban)

fuentes/acuerdo-de-doha/resumen.texto: Agreement signed in Doha on 29 February 2020 by US envoy Zalmay Khalilzad and Taliban political chief Abdul Ghani Baradar. The United States committed to withdrawing all its troops within fourteen months; the Taliban, to preventing al-Qaeda from using Afghanistan against the United States and to negotiating with the Afghan government, which did not take part.

fuentes/acuerdo-de-doha/por_que_importa.texto: The Biden administration completed the withdrawal in August 2021, amid the collapse of the Afghan government and the Taliban's return to power.

fuentes/resolucion-2254/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-2254/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted unanimously on 18 December 2015 that endorsed a roadmap for Syria: negotiations between the government and the opposition, “credible, inclusive and non-sectarian” governance, a new constitution and free elections under UN supervision. It excluded groups deemed terrorist, such as the Islamic State and the al-Nusra Front, from the ceasefire.

fuentes/resolucion-2254/por_que_importa.texto: It was never implemented under Bashar al-Assad; after his fall in December 2024 it continued to be cited as a framework for the Syrian transition.

fuentes/resolucion-2254/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/protocolo-de-minsk/resumen.texto: Twelve-point agreement signed on 5 September 2014 by representatives of Ukraine, Russia and the OSCE and by the leaders of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk republics, after the Ukrainian defeat at Ilovaisk. It provided for an OSCE-monitored ceasefire, the exchange of prisoners, a law on local self-government and the withdrawal of foreign fighters.

fuentes/protocolo-de-minsk/por_que_impor.texto: The ceasefire broke down within a few months and was replaced by the Minsk II agreement.

fuentes/protocolo-de-minsk/leer.0.titulo.texto: Russian text on the OSCE website

fuentes/minsk-ii/resumen.texto: Thirteen-point “Package of Measures” signed on 12 February 2015 in Minsk, after a summit of the leaders of Germany, France, Russia and Ukraine and in the midst of the Battle of Debaltseve. It provided for a ceasefire, the withdrawal of heavy weapons, a Ukrainian constitutional reform with special status for parts of Donetsk and Luhansk and, after local elections, the return of control of its border to Ukraine. The Security Council endorsed it in Resolution 2202.

fuentes/minsk-ii/por_que_importa.texto: It was never fulfilled: Ukraine and Russia accused each other, and Russia declared it over when it recognized the separatist republics on 21 February 2022. Merkel and Hollande's later statements that it gave Ukraine time to strengthen itself are used by Moscow as proof of Western bad faith.

fuentes/minsk-ii/leer.0.titulo.texto: Security Council Resolution 2202 with the text of the agreement annexed

fuentes/resolucion-68-262/idioma_origina.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-68-262/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted on 27 March 2014 by 100 votes in favor, 11 against and 58 abstentions, after Russia vetoed a similar text in the Security Council. It affirms Ukraine's sovereignty and internationally recognized borders and declares that the 16 March referendum in Crimea and Sevastopol has no validity.

fuentes/resolucion-68-262/por_que_import.texto: It is the position of most of the international community on Crimea, although the number of abstentions showed its limits.

fuentes/resolucion-68-262/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-sobre-crimea/t.texto: Putin's speech on the incorporation of Crimea

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-sobre-crimea/r.texto: Speech of 18 March 2014 to both chambers of the Russian parliament and the regional governors, in the Kremlin, before signing the treaty incorporating Crimea and Sevastopol into Russia. He argued that Crimea had always been part of Russia, that its transfer to Ukraine in 1954 was illegitimate and that there had been a coup in Kyiv, and compared the referendum to Kosovo's independence.

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-sobre-crimea/p.texto: It sets out the Russian justification for the annexation, which Ukraine and most states reject as a violation of international law.

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-sobre-crimea/l.texto: English translation on the Kremlin website

fuentes/sobre-la-unidad-historica/titulo.texto: On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians

fuentes/sobre-la-unidad-historica/resume.texto: Article signed by Putin and published on 12 July 2021 in Russian and Ukrainian on the Kremlin website. It argues that Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians are “one people” descended from Kievan Rus', that modern Ukraine is largely a creation of the Soviet era and that its true sovereignty is possible only in partnership with Russia.

fuentes/sobre-la-unidad-historica/por_qu.texto: Many historians read it as an advance justification for the 2022 invasion; Ukrainian historians and many Western ones reject its claims.

fuentes/sobre-la-unidad-historica/leer.0.texto: English translation on the Kremlin website

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-del-24-de-febr.texto: Televised address in the early hours of 24 February 2022, minutes before the first strikes, in which Putin announced a “special military operation” to “demilitarize and denazify” Ukraine and protect the population of the Donbas from an alleged “genocide”. He blamed NATO's eastward expansion and warned that anyone who tried to interfere would face consequences “never seen in history”.
Russia never formally declared war. Ukraine and most governments rejected his arguments as pretexts for a war of aggression, and the General Assembly condemned it a week later.
English translation on the Kremlin website

fuentes/resolucion-es-11-1/idioma_origin.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-es-11-1/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted on 2 March 2022 at an emergency special session convened because Russia had vetoed a text in the Security Council. With 141 votes in favor, 5 against (Russia, Belarus, Syria, North Korea and Eritrea) and 35 abstentions, including those of China and India, it deplores Russia's aggression and demands the immediate, complete and unconditional withdrawal of its forces.

fuentes/resolucion-es-11-1/por_que_impor.texto: It measures Russia's isolation at the UN, although it is not binding and the abstentions showed that much of the Global South was not taking sides.

fuentes/resolucion-es-11-1/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/resolucion-2774/idioma_original.texto: English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

fuentes/resolucion-2774/resumen.texto: Resolution submitted by the United States and adopted on 24 February 2025, the third anniversary of the invasion, with ten votes in favor and five abstentions (Denmark, France, Greece, Slovenia and the United Kingdom). In a few lines it mourns the tragic loss of life in the Russia–Ukraine conflict and calls for a swift end to it and a lasting peace, without naming Russia as the aggressor or mentioning Ukraine's territorial integrity.

fuentes/resolucion-2774/por_que_importa.texto: It was the Council's first substantive resolution on the war and showed the shift under the Trump administration: European countries criticized it for not condemning Russia, which accepted it.

fuentes/resolucion-2774/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the UN document system

fuentes/subir-a-por-aire/resumen.texto: Novel written by George Orwell between September 1938 and March 1939, during a convalescence in French Morocco, and published by Victor Gollancz on 12 June 1939. George Bowling, a 45-year-old insurance salesman, foresees the war to come and returns to the village of his childhood, Lower Binfield, to recover lost innocence. He laments that commerce, speculative builders and capitalism are destroying rural England, and he senses the emergence of new external national threats.

fuentes/subir-a-por-aire/por_que_importa.texto: It is Orwell’s last novel published by Gollancz and the one that precedes Animal Farm: a portrait of England on the eve of the Second World War, written by an author who had already fought in the Spanish Civil War.

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin-de-1945/ti.texto: Berlin Declaration on the Defeat of Germany

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin-de-1945/au.texto: Zhukov, Eisenhower, Montgomery and de Lattre de Tassigny

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin-de-1945/re.texto: Declaration of 5 June 1945 by which the governments of the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France assumed “supreme authority” over Germany after its defeat. It has 15 articles: the first eight deal with military surrender, Article 11 provides for the arrest and trial of Nazi leaders and alleged war criminals, and Article 13 gives the Allies almost unrestricted authority over the civil, economic and legal structures of their zones. It was signed by the four commanders in chief. Zhukov objected to Article 10, on the arrest of Japanese when the USSR was not at war with Japan, and Eisenhower had the clause removed.

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin-de-1945/po.texto: It was the legal basis of the occupation. Its thesis that the German state had ceased to exist, and the power to reform its institutions, in tension with the Hague Conventions, were disputed by jurists; in 2005 the European Court of Human Rights considered the occupation a “sui generis occupation” that conferred sovereign powers on the Allies.

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin-de-1945/le.texto: English text in the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/tratado-de-funcionamiento-de-la-.texto: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Member states of the European Union
The official languages of the Union

One of the two founding treaties of the European Union, together with the Treaty on European Union. It began as the 1957 Treaty of Rome that created the European Economic Community, lost the word “Economic” with the 1992 Maastricht Treaty, and received its current name with the Treaty of Lisbon, signed on 13 December 2007 after the failure of the European Constitution in the 2005 referendums, and in force since 2009. It sets out the Union’s competences and the functioning of its institutions and policies; the common foreign and security policy is in the other treaty.
It is the text with the most detailed legal framework for the Union’s policies. In 2011 a paragraph was added to Article 136 allowing the creation of a stability mechanism for the euro area.
Consolidated 2010 version published in the Official Journal of the EU (copy from the BOE)

fuentes/resolucion-82/resumen.texto: Resolution of 25 June 1950, the day of the North Korean invasion, adopted by nine votes in favor, none against, and with Yugoslavia abstaining. It condemned the “armed attack” on the Republic of Korea and called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and the withdrawal of North Korean forces to the 38th parallel. The Soviet Union was absent because it had been boycotting the Council since January, in protest at the fact that China’s seat was held by the government of Taiwan. North Korea ignored it.

fuentes/resolucion-82/por_que_importa.texto: First Security Council resolution on the Korean War; it was followed by Resolutions 83 and 84.

fuentes/resolucion-82/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the United Nations document system

fuentes/resolucion-84/resumen.texto: Resolution of 7 July 1950 that recommended that UN members place their forces and assistance at the disposal of a unified command under the United States, which would appoint the commander and could use the United Nations flag, and asked Washington for reports. It was adopted by seven votes in favor; Egypt, India and Yugoslavia abstained and the Soviet Union remained absent.

fuentes/resolucion-84/por_que_importa.texto: It gave rise to the United Nations Command in Korea.

fuentes/resolucion-84/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text in the United Nations document system

fuentes/constitucion-francesa-de-1958/ti.texto: Constitution of the French Fifth Republic

fuentes/constitucion-francesa-de-1958/au.texto: Michel Debré and Charles de Gaulle

fuentes/constitucion-francesa-de-1958/re.texto: French Constitution of 4 October 1958, approved by referendum on 28 September. It replaced the Constitution of the Fourth Republic, of 1946, from which it kept the preamble, and created a semi-presidential system with a strong executive. It was drafted under the direction of Michel Debré; De Gaulle, called back from his retirement when a coup linked to the Algerian War came close, was its main promoter.

fuentes/constitucion-francesa-de-1958/po.texto: It was born out of the crisis of the Algerian War. In 1962 De Gaulle used Article 11 to put to referendum the direct election of the president, a highly controversial procedure.

fuentes/constitucion-francesa-de-1958/le.texto: Current text on the website of the Constitutional Council

fuentes/discurso-del-imperio-del-mal/res.texto: Speech by Ronald Reagan on 8 March 1983 to the National Association of Evangelicals, in Orlando, during the Cold War and the Soviet-Afghan War. He called the Soviet Union an “evil empire” and “the focus of evil in the modern world,” rejected the idea that both superpowers were equally responsible for the arms race, and warned supporters of a nuclear freeze against the temptation to place themselves above everything else. The phrase had been proposed by its writer, Anthony Dolan.

fuentes/discurso-del-imperio-del-mal/por.texto: The press of the time criticized it as incendiary, and the TASS agency spoke of “lunatic and bellicose anticommunism”; the historian John Lewis Gaddis sees it as the close of a rhetorical offensive against détente. In 1988, in Moscow, Reagan said he no longer thought that way: it was “another time, another era.”

fuentes/la-segunda-guerra-mundial-de-chu.texto: Winston Churchill’s six-volume war memoirs, published between 1948 and 1953, covering the period from the end of the First World War to July 1945. Churchill composed them with a team of collaborators, “the Syndicate,” based on his notes and privileged access to official documents, with the text revised by the Cabinet Secretary.

It is the incomplete memoir of a protagonist, written from his own point of view and unable to reveal facts such as the use of Ultra. The historian David Reynolds notes that Churchill skipped the 1920s because they did not sustain his image as a visionary, and that his portrait of the Soviet Union changed with the circumstances. Churchill received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

fuentes/orden-ejecutiva-9066/resumen.texto: Order signed on 19 February 1942, two months after Pearl Harbor, which authorized the Secretary of War and military commanders to establish military zones from which “any or all persons” could be excluded. It did not name the Japanese, but it was used to expel about 125,000 people of Japanese descent from the West Coast, two-thirds of them American citizens, and send them to relocation camps in the interior.

fuentes/orden-ejecutiva-9066/por_que_imp.texto: German and Italian Americans who were interned were held under other rules. In 1976 President Ford formally ended the order and apologized.

fuentes/orden-ejecutiva-9066/leer.0.titu.texto: Text and context at the United States National Archives

fuentes/discurso-de-putin-en-munich-2007.texto: Putin’s speech at the Munich Security Conference

Speech of 10 February 2007, the first by a Russian head of state at that conference, to which he was invited by its chairman, Horst Teltschik. Putin criticized the unipolar model—“one center of power, one center of force, one center of decision-making”—the almost unrestrained use of force by the United States, the enlargement of NATO toward Russia’s borders and plans for missile shields, and said that only the UN can authorize the use of force.

The Russian press called it “historic” and “prophetic.” US senator Joe Lieberman said that its rhetoric sounded more like the Cold War, and Defense Secretary Robert Gates replied that “no one wants a new Cold War with Russia”; Horst Teltschik, who had invited him, interpreted it as an expression of deep frustration. The historian Jonathan Haslam links it to the turn that followed the Iraq War and Ukraine’s Orange Revolution.
English transcript on the Kremlin website

fuentes/nuevo-start/resumen.texto: Treaty on the reduction of strategic nuclear weapons, signed in Prague on 8 April 2010 and in force since 5 February 2011. It replaced the Treaty of Moscow (SORT) and limited each party to 1,550 deployed strategic warheads, with an inspection and verification regime. It was extended in February 2021; Russia suspended its participation on 21 February 2023 without withdrawing, and the treaty expired on 5 February 2026.

fuentes/nuevo-start/por_que_importa.texto: It was negotiated after START I expired in December 2009; its extension was thrown into doubt when the United States announced its withdrawal from the INF Treaty.

fuentes/nuevo-start/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text on the US State Department website

fuentes/texto-del-tratado-de-lausana/res.texto: Peace treaty signed on 24 July 1923 at Lausanne between Turkey, Greece and the Allied powers of the First World War. It replaced the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres, which the Turkish National Movement had rejected, recognized the sovereignty of the Republic of Turkey and fixed its borders with Greece and Bulgaria; a separate convention regulated the straits. Its Annex VIII, the Declaration of Amnesty, granted immunity for acts committed between 1914 and 1922 for military or political motives.

fuentes/texto-del-tratado-de-lausana/por.texto: It defined the map of modern Turkey and closed the possibility of prosecuting Ottoman war crimes. It entered into force on 6 August 1924.

fuentes/texto-del-tratado-de-lausana/lee.texto: Text of the treaty in the World War I document archive of Brigham Young University
