fuentes/texto-de-la-convencion-sobre-los.texto: Convention on the Rights of the Child
English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

Human rights treaty adopted by the UN General Assembly on 20 November 1989, which establishes the civil, political, economic, social, health and cultural rights of children and defines a child as any person under 18 years of age, unless national law sets an earlier age of majority. States parties must act in the best interests of the child and report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child. Its 2000 optional protocols restrict the participation of minors in armed conflict and prohibit their sale and sexual exploitation; the third, from 2011, allows individual complaints.
It is the human rights treaty with the most states parties: all UN members except the United States.
Text of the Convention on the UNICEF website

fuentes/texto-del-pacto-de-derechos-civi.texto: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
English, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese and Arabic

Treaty adopted by the UN General Assembly on 16 December 1966 (resolution 2200 A) and in force since 23 March 1976. It recognizes the rights to life, freedom of religion, expression and assembly, electoral rights and due process guarantees; its Article 6 does not prohibit the death penalty but restricts it to the most serious crimes. The Human Rights Committee monitors compliance, and the second optional protocol abolished the death penalty, with a possible reservation for military crimes committed in wartime.

Together with the Universal Declaration and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, it forms the International Bill of Human Rights. It has 175 states parties (as of December 2025); China and Cuba signed it without ratifying it.
Text of the Covenant in the United Nations treaty collection

fuentes/texto-del-acuerdo-de-schengen/ti.texto: Schengen Agreement and its Implementing Convention

fuentes/texto-del-acuerdo-de-schengen/re.texto: Agreement signed on 14 June 1985 at Schengen (Luxembourg) by Belgium, France, West Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands to gradually abolish controls at their common borders, including reducing vehicle checks and harmonizing visa policies. The 1990 Implementing Convention provided for the elimination of systematic controls at internal borders and the establishment of a common visa policy.

fuentes/texto-del-acuerdo-de-schengen/po.texto: It created the Schengen area, which the Treaty of Amsterdam incorporated into European Union law in 1999.

fuentes/texto-del-acuerdo-de-schengen/le.texto: Text of the 1990 Implementing Convention on Wikisource

personas/francisco-fernando/resumen.texto: Archduke and heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne from 1896. His assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, together with his wife Sophie, set off the crisis that led to the First World War.

personas/gavrilo-princip/resumen.texto: Bosnian Serb student from the Young Bosnia organization, armed by the Serbian secret society Black Hand, who killed Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. Because he was under twenty he was not sentenced to death, and he died of tuberculosis in Theresienstadt prison.

personas/francisco-jose/resumen.texto: Emperor of Austria from 1848 and King of Hungary from 1867 until his death in 1916. He signed the declaration of war on Serbia and the manifesto “To My Peoples” of July 1914.

personas/guillermo-ii/resumen.texto: Last German Emperor and King of Prussia (1888-1918). In July 1914 he gave Austria-Hungary unconditional backing, the so-called “blank cheque”; he abdicated in November 1918 and died in exile in the Netherlands.

personas/nicolas-ii/resumen.texto: Last Tsar of Russia (1894-1917). His general mobilization order of July 1914 precipitated the German declaration of war; he abdicated after the February Revolution of 1917 and was shot with his family by the Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg in 1918.

personas/berchtold/resumen.texto: Foreign Minister of Austria-Hungary from 1912 to 1915. He pushed for the ultimatum to Serbia and signed the telegram declaring war on 28 July 1914.

personas/bethmann-hollweg/resumen.texto: Chancellor of the German Empire from 1909 to 1917. He directed German diplomacy during the July Crisis and, speaking to the British ambassador, called the 1839 treaty guaranteeing Belgian neutrality “a scrap of paper”.

personas/edward-grey/resumen.texto: British Foreign Secretary from 1905 to 1916. On 3 August 1914 he made the case in the Commons for entering the war, and the next day he sent the ultimatum to Germany over Belgian neutrality; he is credited with the phrase “the lamps are going out all over Europe”.

personas/arthur-zimmermann/resumen.texto: German Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in 1916 and 1917. His telegram proposing to Mexico an alliance against the United States was intercepted by the British and helped bring the United States into the war.

personas/woodrow-wilson/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1913 to 1921. He led his country into the First World War in 1917, set out the Fourteen Points and promoted the League of Nations, whose membership the US Senate did not approve. Nobel Peace Prize 1919.

personas/lloyd-george/resumen.texto: British Prime Minister from 1916 to 1922, heading a coalition government during the second half of the First World War. He was one of the “Big Four” at the Paris Peace Conference.

personas/clemenceau/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of France from 1906 to 1909 and from 1917 to 1920, nicknamed “the Tiger”. He led France in the final year of the war and presided over the Paris Peace Conference, where he argued for harsh terms for Germany.

personas/aristide-briand/resumen.texto: French politician, eleven times prime minister and Foreign Minister from 1925 to 1932. He negotiated the Locarno Treaties, for which he shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with Gustav Stresemann, and proposed the pact renouncing war that bears his name and Kellogg's.

personas/frank-kellogg/resumen.texto: United States Secretary of State from 1925 to 1929. He turned Briand's bilateral proposal into a multilateral pact renouncing war and received the 1929 Nobel Peace Prize.

personas/chamberlain/resumen.texto: British Prime Minister from 1937 to 1940. He embodied the policy of appeasement towards Hitler with the Munich Agreement and, after the invasion of Poland, announced by radio the country's entry into the war on 3 September 1939.

personas/daladier/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of France from 1938 to 1940. He signed the Munich Agreement and, in September 1939, led France into war against Germany.

personas/francisco-franco/resumen.texto: General who from October 1936 led the rebel side in the Spanish Civil War and ruled Spain as dictator from 1939 until his death. Despite his closeness to Hitler and Mussolini, he kept Spain out of the Second World War.

personas/ribbentrop/resumen.texto: Foreign Minister of Nazi Germany from 1938 to 1945. He signed the pact with Molotov in 1939 and delivered the declaration of war on the United States in 1941; convicted at Nuremberg, he was hanged in 1946.

personas/molotov/resumen.texto: People's Commissar and later Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR (1939-1949 and 1953-1956). He signed the non-aggression pact with Germany and its secret protocol, announced the German invasion of 1941 on the radio, and took part in the Allied conferences and the founding of the UN.

personas/heydrich/resumen.texto: Head of the Reich Security Main Office and one of the chief organizers of the Holocaust. He convened the Wannsee Conference in January 1942 and died that same year after an attack by the Czechoslovak resistance in Prague.

personas/eichmann/resumen.texto: SS officer who organized the deportation of millions of Jews to the ghettos and extermination camps and drafted the minutes of Wannsee. He fled to Argentina, where Mossad abducted him in 1960; tried in Jerusalem, he was hanged in 1962.

personas/churchill/resumen.texto: British Prime Minister from 1940 to 1945 and from 1951 to 1955. He led British resistance against Nazi Germany, signed the Atlantic Charter, took part in Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam, and in 1946 popularized the image of the “iron curtain”. Nobel Prize in Literature 1953.

personas/franklin-roosevelt/nacimiento.l.texto: Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site

personas/franklin-roosevelt/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1933 to 1945, the only one elected four times. He signed the Atlantic Charter with Churchill, led his country into the war after Pearl Harbor and conceived the United Nations; he died weeks before the end of the war in Europe.

personas/de-gaulle/resumen.texto: French general who, after the defeat of 1940, called from London for the fight to continue and led Free France. He founded the Fifth Republic in 1958, served as its president until 1969 and negotiated the end of the Algerian War.

personas/hirohito/resumen.texto: Emperor of Japan from 1926 to 1989. He reigned during Japanese expansion in Asia and the Pacific War, and on 15 August 1945 announced the surrender on the radio; the American occupation decided not to try him, and the extent of his responsibility for the war is still debated.

personas/hideki-tojo/resumen.texto: General and Prime Minister of Japan from 1941 to 1944, heading the government that decided on the attack on Pearl Harbor. Sentenced to death by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, he was hanged in 1948.

personas/eisenhower/resumen.texto: American general, Supreme Allied Commander in Western Europe, who directed the Normandy landings. He was the first Supreme Allied Commander of NATO and President of the United States from 1953 to 1961; in his farewell address he warned about the “military-industrial complex”.

personas/douglas-macarthur/resumen.texto: American general who commanded the Allies in the South West Pacific, accepted Japan's surrender and directed its occupation. While he was leading UN forces in Korea, Truman relieved him in 1951 over disagreements about extending the war to China.

personas/truman/nacimiento.lugar.texto: Harry S Truman Birthplace State Historic Site

personas/truman/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1945 to 1953. He ordered the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, announced in 1947 the doctrine that bears his name, promoted the Marshall Plan and NATO, and led his country into the Korean War.

personas/robert-jackson/resumen.texto: United States Supreme Court justice who served as the chief American prosecutor at the Nuremberg trial. He negotiated the London Charter, and his opening statement is one of the founding texts of international criminal law.

personas/george-kennan/resumen.texto: American diplomat posted in Moscow. His 1946 “Long Telegram” and the 1947 article signed “X” formulated the strategy of “containment” of the Soviet Union, which he later criticized for its militarization.

personas/george-marshall/resumen.texto: Chief of Staff of the US Army in the Second World War and later Secretary of State (1947-1949) and Secretary of Defense. At Harvard he announced the European reconstruction plan that bears his name; Nobel Peace Prize 1953.

personas/eleanor-roosevelt/resumen.texto: First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945 and later a delegate to the UN. She chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

personas/rene-cassin/resumen.texto: French jurist of Free France and one of the principal drafters of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. He presided over the European Court of Human Rights and received the 1968 Nobel Peace Prize.

personas/raphael-lemkin/resumen.texto: Polish Jewish jurist who coined the word “genocide” in 1944, with the extermination of the Armenians and that of the Jews in mind, and devoted the rest of his life to securing the UN convention that made it a crime in 1948.

personas/nehru/resumen.texto: Leader of the Indian National Congress and Prime Minister of India from independence in 1947 until his death. He delivered the midnight speech at independence and was one of the driving forces behind the Non-Aligned Movement.

personas/robert-schuman/resumen.texto: Foreign Minister of France from 1948 to 1952. On 9 May 1950 he proposed pooling Franco-German coal and steel production, the origin of the European Communities.

personas/kim-il-sung/resumen.texto: Founder of North Korea, which he ruled from 1948 until his death. With the backing of Stalin and Mao he launched the invasion of the South in June 1950 that started the Korean War.

personas/ho-chi-minh/resumen.texto: Vietnamese communist leader who founded the Viet Minh, proclaimed Vietnam's independence in 1945 and led the war against France. He was president of North Vietnam until his death, in the midst of the war against South Vietnam and the United States.

personas/jruschov/resumen.texto: First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964. He denounced Stalin's crimes in the 1956 “Secret Speech”, crushed the Hungarian Revolution that same year and was, with Kennedy, a central figure in the Cuban Missile Crisis.

personas/imre-nagy/resumen.texto: Reformist Hungarian communist, prime minister in 1953-1955 and during the 1956 revolution, when he announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. After the Soviet invasion he was tried in secret and executed in 1958.

personas/kennedy/nacimiento.lugar.texto: John Fitzgerald Kennedy National Historic Site

personas/kennedy/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1961 to 1963. He faced the Bay of Pigs fiasco, the building of the Berlin Wall and the Cuban Missile Crisis; he was assassinated in Dallas in November 1963.

personas/lyndon-johnson/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1963 to 1969. He obtained the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution from Congress in 1964 and raised the American presence in Vietnam to more than half a million troops.

personas/alexander-dubcek/resumen.texto: First Secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia in 1968 and champion of the “socialism with a human face” of the Prague Spring, crushed by the Warsaw Pact invasion in August of that year.

personas/brezhnev/resumen.texto: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1964 to 1982. He ordered the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, signed the Helsinki Final Act in 1975 and sent the Soviet army into Afghanistan in 1979.

personas/reagan/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989. He revived the arms race and called the USSR an “evil empire”, but later negotiated the INF Treaty with Gorbachev; in 1987, in Berlin, he called for the wall to be torn down.

personas/thatcher/resumen.texto: British Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, the first woman to hold the office. She led the 1982 Falklands War, was a close ally of Reagan in the final stage of the Cold War and backed the military response to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait.

personas/gorbachov/resumen.texto: Last leader of the Soviet Union (1985-1991). His reforms, perestroika and glasnost, and his refusal to intervene in Eastern Europe hastened the end of the Cold War; he signed the INF Treaty with Reagan and received the 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.

personas/george-h-w-bush/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1989 to 1993, during the end of the Cold War and German reunification. He led the UN-authorized coalition that drove Iraq out of Kuwait in 1991.

personas/saddam-hussein/resumen.texto: President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. He started the war against Iran in 1980 and the invasion of Kuwait in 1990; overthrown by the 2003 invasion, he was convicted by an Iraqi court for the Dujail massacre and hanged in 2006.

personas/milosevic/resumen.texto: President of Serbia and later of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the wars of the 1990s. Handed over to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, he died in 2006 in his cell in The Hague before his trial for war crimes and genocide had ended.

personas/ratko-mladic/resumen.texto: Commander of the Bosnian Serb army in the 1992-1995 war. A fugitive for almost sixteen years, he was arrested in Serbia in 2011; the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia sentenced him in 2017 to life imprisonment for genocide in Srebrenica and other crimes, and he died in custody in The Hague in 2026.

personas/kofi-annan/resumen.texto: Ghanaian diplomat, head of UN peacekeeping operations during the Rwanda and Bosnia crises and Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006. He shared the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize with the organization and in 2004 described the invasion of Iraq as illegal under the Charter.

personas/tony-blair/resumen.texto: British Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007. He took the United Kingdom into the Kosovo War, the war in Afghanistan and, alongside Bush, the 2003 invasion of Iraq, for which the Chilcot Inquiry criticized his government in 2016.

personas/george-w-bush/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 2001 to 2009. After the 11 September attacks he launched the “war on terror”, the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and that of Iraq in 2003, justified by weapons of mass destruction that were never found.

personas/putin/resumen.texto: Former KGB officer, president of Russia since 2000, with an interval as prime minister between 2008 and 2012. He ordered the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the invasion of Ukraine in 2022; since 2023 he has been subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, which Russia does not recognize.

personas/zelenski/resumen.texto: Actor and comedian who won the presidency of Ukraine in 2019 with 73% of the vote. He has led the country's defence since the Russian invasion of 2022; his term was due to end in 2024, but martial law prevents elections, and Russia uses this argument to question his legitimacy.

personas/william-howard-taft/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1909 to 1913 and, from 1921 to 1930, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court: the only person to hold both offices. His administration pursued antitrust cases (Standard Oil and American Tobacco, which the Court decided in favor of the government in 1911) and practiced “dollar diplomacy,” with the occupation of Nicaragua (1912–1933). In 1912 Theodore Roosevelt challenged him for the nomination, the Republican Party split, and Taft, with only two states (Utah and Vermont), lost to Woodrow Wilson.

personas/warren-harding/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1921 until his death on 2 August 1923 in San Francisco. He promised a “return to normalcy” after the war, promoted the Washington Naval Conference of 1921–1922, which limited the navies of the great powers, and freed prisoners convicted for opposing World War I. After his death, scandals in his government came to light, such as Teapot Dome, for which his Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, was convicted.

personas/calvin-coolidge/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1923 to 1929. He took office on Harding’s death and did not seek re-election in 1928. In 1924 he signed the law that granted citizenship to all Native Americans and the immigration law that limited entry from outside the Western Hemisphere and explicitly excluded Japanese immigration. During his term the Kellogg–Briand Pact (1928) was signed and taxes were reduced.

personas/herbert-hoover/resumen.texto: Mining engineer who organized food relief for occupied Belgium in 1914 and, after the war, for Central and Eastern Europe, and who served as Secretary of Commerce under Harding and Coolidge. President of the United States from 1929 to 1933, he faced the 1929 crash and the Great Depression: his response, which included the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, was judged insufficient, and he lost to Franklin Roosevelt in 1932. On 28 July 1932 he ordered the army to clear the Bonus Army encampment in Washington; MacArthur went further and destroyed the one at Anacostia, and Hoover later backed him.

personas/nixon/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1969 to 1974. From March 1969 he ordered the secret bombing of Cambodia; he withdrew combat troops from Vietnam in 1973, traveled to China in 1972 and signed the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with the USSR. He secretly backed Pakistan in the 1971 Bangladesh war and led a covert campaign against Allende in Chile. Because of the Watergate scandal he resigned on 9 August 1974, the only US president to do so.

personas/gerald-ford/nacimiento.lugar.texto: Gerald R. Ford Birthsite and Gardens

personas/gerald-ford/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1974 to 1977. He was appointed vice president in 1973 under the 25th Amendment after Spiro Agnew’s resignation, took office on 9 August 1974 when Nixon resigned, and was never elected to either office. On 8 September 1974 he pardoned Nixon, a much-debated decision. He signed the Helsinki Final Act in 1975; during his term Saigon fell (April 1975), and he gave his approval to the Indonesian invasion of East Timor. He lost to Jimmy Carter in 1976.

personas/jimmy-carter/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1977 to 1981. He negotiated the Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel, the Panama Canal Treaties and SALT II (signed in 1979 and never ratified), and established diplomatic relations with China. His term was marked by the seizure of hostages at the US embassy in Tehran (52 Americans, 444 days) and by the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, which ended détente and led to the boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics. The CIA had been aiding the mujahideen since July 1979, and from 1980 it armed them through Pakistan’s ISI, with Saudi funds. He lost to Ronald Reagan, chaired the Carter Center, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002, and died on 29 December 2024, aged 100.

personas/bill-clinton/nacimiento.lugar.texto: President William Jefferson Clinton Birthplace Home National Historic Site

personas/bill-clinton/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 1993 to 2001. In 1993 he had the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) with Canada and Mexico ratified, together with two parallel side agreements; the treaty had been signed by Bush in December 1992. He supported NATO enlargement, intervened in Bosnia (Dayton Accords, 1995) and in 1999 in Kosovo, with a NATO bombing campaign that lacked authorization from the UN Security Council. He did not intervene in the Rwandan genocide of 1994, which he later considered one of his greatest failures. In December 1998 the House of Representatives impeached him for perjury and obstruction of justice in the Lewinsky case, and the Senate acquitted him in February 1999.

personas/barack-obama/nacimiento.lugar.texto: Kapiolani Medical Center for Women and Children

personas/barack-obama/resumen.texto: First African American president of the United States, from 2009 to 2017, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2009. He responded to the 2008 financial crisis with a stimulus package and the Dodd-Frank reform, and signed the health law known as Obamacare. In foreign policy he sent more troops to Afghanistan in 2009, completed the withdrawal from Iraq in 2011, and returned to Iraq and Syria in 2014 against the Islamic State. He ordered the operation that killed Osama bin Laden, intervened in Libya, negotiated the nuclear agreement with Iran (2015), restored relations with Cuba, and expanded air strikes and the use of special forces.

personas/yuri-andropov/resumen.texto: Chairman of the KGB from 1967 to 1982 and Soviet ambassador to Hungary from 1954 to 1957, where he played a central role in the repression of the 1956 revolution. As KGB chief he created the Fifth Directorate against dissent and expanded the psychiatric confinement of dissidents (Sakharov, Medvedev, Sharansky). In 1968 he called for “extreme measures” against Czechoslovakia, and in 1979 he was among those who decided to invade Afghanistan. He was general secretary of the CPSU from 12 November 1982 until his death on 9 February 1984. During his brief term he pursued corruption and absenteeism at work, and the Cold War deepened, with the downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 (1 September 1983, 269 dead) and the breakdown of nuclear arms negotiations.

personas/konstantin-chernenko/resumen.texto: A collaborator of Brezhnev from 1950 in Moldavia, he was elected general secretary of the CPSU on 13 February 1984, after Andropov’s death, and in April became chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet. With his health failing, he governed together with Defense Minister Dmitry Ustinov and Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko. In May 1984 the USSR announced it would not attend the Los Angeles Olympics, a year after the Western boycott of the Moscow Games. He died on 10 March 1985 and was succeeded by Gorbachev.

personas/vladimir-ivashko/resumen.texto: Ukrainian communist leader, first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine from 1989 and, from July 1990, deputy general secretary of the CPSU. He was acting general secretary of the CPSU from 24 to 29 August 1991: Gorbachev resigned from the post after the failure of the coup, and on the 29th the Supreme Soviet suspended the party’s activities. He retired in 1992 and died in 1994.

personas/mikoyan/resumen.texto: Soviet leader of Armenian origin. In 1956 he collaborated with Khrushchev on the “secret speech” and, sent to Budapest with Suslov during the Hungarian revolution, opposed the use of Soviet troops. He was the first senior Soviet official to visit revolutionary Cuba and in November 1962 travelled to Havana to persuade Castro to accept the withdrawal of the missiles after the crisis; he chaired the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet between July 1964 and December 1965. On 5 March 1940 he was one of the six Politburo members who approved the order to shoot some 25,700 Polish prisoners (the Katyn massacre).

personas/gromiko/resumen.texto: Soviet diplomat: ambassador to the United States from 1943, delegate at the Tehran, Dumbarton Oaks, Yalta and Potsdam conferences, representative to the UN, where his frequent use of the veto earned him the nickname “Mr. Nyet,” and minister of foreign affairs from 1957 to 1985. He met Kennedy during the Cuban Missile Crisis and led Soviet foreign policy during détente, including the nuclear non-proliferation and partial test ban treaties. He chaired the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet from 1985 to 1988.

personas/voroshilov/resumen.texto: Soviet marshal and People’s Commissar for Defense from 1934. He commanded Soviet troops in the Winter War against Finland (November 1939 to January 1940), with heavy losses, and was relieved of his command; in 1941 he could not prevent the German siege of Leningrad. During the Great Purge he personally signed 185 documented execution lists. On 5 March 1940 he was one of the six Politburo members who approved the order to shoot some 25,700 Polish prisoners (the Katyn massacre). He chaired the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, as head of state, from 1953 to 1960.

personas/malenkov/resumen.texto: Soviet leader, member of the State Defense Committee during the war and head of the missile program. On Stalin’s death in March 1953 he succeeded him as prime minister, until he was forced to resign in February 1955. He declared that “a new world war with modern weapons would mean the end of world civilization” and defended peaceful coexistence with the United States without loosening Soviet control over Eastern Europe, although he had to qualify this after criticism from Khrushchev and Molotov.

personas/kosygin/resumen.texto: Chairman of the Soviet Council of Ministers from 1964 to 1980. He mediated between India and Pakistan at the 1966 Tashkent Declaration, met Lyndon Johnson at the Glassboro summit, where no agreement was reached to limit antiballistic missiles, travelled to Beijing in 1969 because of the Sino-Soviet tensions, and signed the Treaty of Moscow with West Germany on 12 August 1970.

personas/bulganin/resumen.texto: Soviet marshal and minister of defense, prime minister from February 1955 to 1958. During the 1956 Suez Crisis he sent letters to the governments of the United Kingdom, France and Israel threatening rocket attacks on London, Paris and Tel Aviv if they did not withdraw their forces from Egypt.

personas/kitchener/resumen.texto: British field marshal, Secretary of State for War from August 1914. He foresaw a war of at least three years and organized the largest volunteer army in British history, the “New Armies,” but lost influence among politicians and commanders, who criticized the way he ran the ministry. He died on 5 June 1916 when HMS Hampshire, on which he was travelling to Russia to negotiate with the tsar, struck a German mine. As commander in chief in the Boer War (1900–1902) he inherited and expanded the burning of farms and the concentration camps in which the British confined Boer and African civilians; the historian Caroline Elkins describes his conduct of the war as a scorched-earth policy.

personas/azana/resumen.texto: Spanish politician, head of government of the Second Republic (1931–1933 and 1936) and president of the Republic from 10 May 1936. At the start of the Civil War he entrusted Martínez Barrio with forming a conciliation government, whose attempt at compromise was rejected by General Mola; on 13 September 1936 he authorized Negrín to move the gold reserves, which went to the Soviet Union as payment for arms. He crossed into France in February 1939 and resigned at the end of that month (he sent the letter on 28 February), after France and the United Kingdom recognized Franco’s government, instead of returning to Spain; Negrín sharply criticized this decision before the Permanent Deputation meeting in Paris.

personas/martinez-barrio/resumen.texto: Spanish republican politician, president of the Cortes from March 1936 and acting head of the Republic from 7 April to 10 May. On the night of 18–19 July 1936 Azaña charged him with forming a conciliation government to avert war: he phoned military leaders and spoke with General Mola, who refused any rapprochement (historians such as Hugh Thomas state that he offered him a post in the new government, which he denied in his memoirs). He resigned on 19 July, replaced by José Giral, and from 1945 he presided over the Republic in exile until his death.

personas/donald-trump/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 2017 to 2021 and since January 2025. In his first term he withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement and the Iran nuclear deal, recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel, announced withdrawal from the INF Treaty, presided over the signing of the 2020 Abraham Accords, met Kim Jong-un three times between June 2018 and June 2019 without achieving denuclearization, and agreed with the Taliban in Doha, on 29 February 2020, to the withdrawal of US troops from Afghanistan. In his second term he imposed tariffs on most countries, argued with Zelensky on camera in February 2025, met Putin in Alaska, ordered the strikes of 22 June 2025 against Iranian nuclear facilities, ordered the military operation of 3 January 2026 in Venezuela that captured Nicolás Maduro, which his government justified as a police action with military support, and authorized the joint bombing with Israel of Iran on 28 February 2026, which started a war.

personas/gordon-brown/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Labour leader from 2007 to 2010, First Lord of the Treasury. He maintained the British commitment in Iraq, although he ordered an inquiry into the country’s participation in the war, and in 2009 withdrew 3,700 soldiers from Basra. At the close of the London G-20 summit he announced the leaders of the 20 largest economies’ agreement to ease the financial crisis, with a fund of one trillion dollars; his foreign secretary, David Miliband, represented him at the signing ceremony of the Treaty of Lisbon (13 December 2007).

personas/kuznetsov/resumen.texto: Soviet politician and diplomat: deputy foreign minister from 1955 to 1977, took part in resolving the Cuban Missile Crisis, led the Soviet delegation in the border negotiations with China between 1969 and 1970 after the clash on Damansky Island, and took part in the 1971 Indo-Pakistani crisis. He served as acting head of state, as chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, from November 1982 to June 1983, from February to April 1984 and from March to July 1985.

personas/derby/resumen.texto: British Conservative politician. In October 1915, as Director-General of Recruiting, he instituted the Derby Scheme, an intermediate step between voluntary enlistment and conscription, which did not have the expected success; he was Secretary of State for War from December 1916 to April 1918, ambassador in Paris from 1918 to 1920, during the Peace Conference, and again Secretary of State for War from 1922 to 1924.

personas/theresa-may/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Conservative leader from 2016 to 2019. She began the country’s exit from the European Union by triggering Article 50 in March 2017. After the poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal in March 2018, her government accused Russia of having orchestrated it, and 28 other countries supported the British assessment; together they expelled 153 Russian diplomats, an unprecedented figure, and Russia denied the accusations.

personas/liz-truss/resumen.texto: Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom from 2021 to 2022 and prime minister in September and October 2022, the shortest tenure in British history. On 10 February 2022 she met the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, in Moscow, amid the tensions before the invasion of Ukraine, and before and after the invasion she advocated sanctions against Russia and encouraged other G7 leaders to impose them.

personas/rishi-sunak/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Conservative leader from 2022 to 2024. He authorized aid and arms shipments to Ukraine and signed in Kyiv, on 12 January 2024, the security cooperation agreement with £2.5 billion in military aid. After the attacks of 7 October 2023 he backed Israel’s right to defend itself and later called for a “sustainable” ceasefire in Gaza.

personas/joe-biden/resumen.texto: President of the United States from 2021 to 2025 and vice president under Barack Obama from 2009 to 2017. As a senator he supported the war in Afghanistan and in 2002 voted to authorize the Iraq War; as president he withdrew troops from Afghanistan (the Taliban retook power in August 2021), imposed sanctions on Russia and authorized military aid to Ukraine after the 2022 invasion, and gave military and diplomatic support to Israel in the Gaza war.

personas/boris-johnson/resumen.texto: Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2018 and prime minister from 2019 to 2022. His government carried out the United Kingdom’s exit from the European Union in January 2020 and, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, imposed sanctions on Russia and authorized the shipment of arms and aid to Ukraine.

personas/david-cameron/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2010 to 2016 and Foreign Secretary from November 2023 to July 2024. In 2011 he secured a large parliamentary majority to take part in the military intervention in Libya (Operation Ellamy) and authorized bombing of the Islamic State in Syria; in 2013 he became the first prime minister since 1782 to lose a foreign policy vote in the Commons, on military action against the Syrian government of Bashar al-Assad.

personas/keir-starmer/resumen.texto: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from July 2024 to July 2026 and Labour leader from 2020 to 2026; on 22 June 2026 he announced that he would resign and left office in July, when a new Labour leader was elected. Under his government the United Kingdom reaffirmed its support for Ukraine, and in February 2025 he discussed that support and a possible peace agreement with Donald Trump in Washington.

personas/angela-merkel/resumen.texto: Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021. After Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, which led to international sanctions, she promoted the construction of the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which went ahead despite US sanctions in 2019; in February 2015 she took part in the Minsk summit with the leaders of France, Russia and Ukraine. At the 2008 NATO summit in Bucharest she opposed giving Ukraine and Georgia a Membership Action Plan.

personas/francois-hollande/resumen.texto: President of France from 2012 to 2017. In January 2013 he authorized Operation Serval against Islamist groups in northern Mali, withdrew French troops from Afghanistan, and governed the country during the 2015 Paris attacks; in February 2015 he took part in the Minsk summit with the leaders of Germany, Russia and Ukraine.

personas/emmanuel-macron/resumen.texto: President of France since 2017. Before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 he spoke with Vladimir Putin in person and by phone, and after it he called for keeping dialogue open; on 16 June 2022 he travelled to Kyiv with Olaf Scholz and Mario Draghi and said that neutral countries were making a historic mistake.

personas/nicolas-sarkozy/resumen.texto: President of France from 2007 to 2012. He negotiated the ceasefire in the 2008 Russo-Georgian War and was among the first heads of state to call for the removal of Muammar Gaddafi: on 19 March 2011 he announced French participation in the military intervention in Libya. On 25 September 2025 the Paris Court convicted him at first instance of five years’ imprisonment and a €100,000 fine for criminal conspiracy in the case concerning alleged Libyan financing of his 2007 campaign, and acquitted him of passive corruption, illegal campaign financing and concealment of embezzlement; he was held in custody from 21 October to 10 November 2025 and was released under judicial supervision pending the appeal trial, scheduled for March 2026, so that conviction was not final.

personas/jacques-chirac/resumen.texto: President of France from 1995 to 2007 and prime minister from 1974 to 1976 and from 1986 to 1988. He opposed the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, together with German chancellor Gerhard Schröder, which strained Franco-American relations. In 1995 he resumed nuclear tests at Mururoa, despite international protests, months before signing the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

personas/francois-mitterrand/resumen.texto: President of France from 1981 to 1995. With Chancellor Helmut Kohl he promoted the Maastricht Treaty; he had opposed German reunification but ended up accepting it as inevitable, and France took part in the UN coalition in the Gulf War (1990–1991). His government supported Habyarimana’s government in Rwanda, and France’s role before and during the 1994 genocide is a subject of controversy; in 1985 French agents sank Greenpeace’s Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, killing one person.

personas/helmut-kohl/resumen.texto: Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany from 1982 to 1998, the longest tenure of the postwar period. After the fall of the Berlin Wall he worked to achieve German unity, realized in the 1990 reunification, and with Mitterrand was the architect of the Maastricht Treaty.

personas/konrad-adenauer/resumen.texto: First chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, from 1949 to 1963. He brought the country into NATO, promoted rearmament and reconciliation with France, and signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957; he did not recognize the German Democratic Republic or the Oder-Neisse line as the border with Poland.

personas/willy-brandt/resumen.texto: Social Democratic leader, mayor of West Berlin and chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany from 1969 to 1974. His Ostpolitik sought to improve relations with the Soviet Union, Poland and the German Democratic Republic, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971; he was criticized from the right for that policy and from the left for not speaking out on the Vietnam War until 1973.

personas/gerhard-schroeder/resumen.texto: Chancellor of Germany from 1998 to 2005. He sent troops to Kosovo and Afghanistan, the first German combat deployments since the Second World War, and together with Chirac refused to join the 2003 invasion of Iraq. After leaving office he worked for Russian state-owned energy companies (Nord Stream, Rosneft, Gazprom) and was criticized for it after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022; in March 2023 an SPD arbitration committee ruled that he had not violated the party’s rules.

personas/olaf-scholz/resumen.texto: Chancellor of Germany from December 2021 to 2025. Three days after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine he announced in his Zeitenwende speech (27 February 2022) the shipment of arms to Ukraine and a €100 billion fund for the Bundeswehr; the large investment in defense was a turning point in German foreign policy.

personas/ursula-von-der-leyen/resumen.texto: German Minister of Defence from 2013 to 2019 and President of the European Commission since 2019. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 she travelled to Kyiv (8 April) and said that Ukraine belonged to the European family, although there was a long way to go before its accession to the Union.

personas/henry-kissinger/resumen.texto: National Security Advisor (1969–1975) and Secretary of State (1973–1977) of the United States under Nixon and Ford. He promoted détente with the Soviet Union, the rapprochement with China and the Paris Peace Accords on Vietnam, for which he received the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize amid controversy. In June 1971 he discussed with Nixon supporting a coup in Bolivia, and in July the 40 Committee approved secret funds for the opposition to President Torres; he backed the Argentine military junta, Indonesia in its invasion of East Timor, and Pakistan in 1971, despite the cable from consul Archer Blood speaking of “selective genocide.” Christopher Hitchens, in his book The Trial of Henry Kissinger (2001), argues that he deserves to be tried for war crimes and crimes against humanity, for acts in Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Bangladesh, Chile, Cyprus and East Timor.

personas/boris-yeltsin/resumen.texto: First president of the Russian Federation, from 1991 to 1999. In August 1991 he resisted the coup against Gorbachev, and his alliance with other national leaders was decisive in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December of that year; in 1993 he ordered the dissolution of Parliament, for which the Constitution did not empower him, and loyal troops stormed the building. In December 1994 he ordered the invasion of Chechnya (the First Chechen War) and in 1996 withdrew federal forces after a peace agreement that gave the republic greater autonomy but not independence.

personas/dmitri-medvedev/resumen.texto: President of Russia from 2008 to 2012, prime minister from 2012 to 2020, and since then deputy chairman of the Security Council. During his presidency Russia fought the 2008 Georgian War and signed the New START treaty with the United States; in February 2022 he said that Russia could withdraw from dialogue on nuclear stability and from New START.

personas/alexandr-lukashenko/resumen.texto: President of Belarus since 1994, the first and so far the only one. In February 2022 he allowed Russian forces to launch part of the invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian territory, and in June 2023 he said he had negotiated with Yevgeny Prigozhin the end of the Wagner Group mutiny; the United States, the European Union and other countries sanctioned him for his support of the war.

personas/josip-broz-tito/resumen.texto: Supreme commander of the Yugoslav Partisans in the Second World War and head of communist Yugoslavia until his death, first as prime minister and from 1953 as president. He broke with Stalin and the Cominform in 1948 and co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement; his government was a one-party state. In the autumn of 1944 the communist leadership decided to expel the ethnic Germans from Yugoslavia, with 70 camps; during the repatriations at Bleiburg (1945) Partisan units committed atrocities, for which the Tito leadership was later blamed; and from 1948 it repressed opponents and suspected sympathizers of the Soviet Union, with the Goli Otok camp, where 16,554 people were imprisoned between 1948 and 1956 according to a 1964 figure from the Yugoslav government, and fewer than 600 died.

personas/joseph-goebbels/resumen.texto: Minister of Propaganda of Nazi Germany from 1933 and Gauleiter of Berlin. After the assassination of the diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris in November 1938, he had antisemitic material published in the press and launched the pogrom of Kristallnacht; he pressed Hitler for “total war” and in 1944 was appointed plenipotentiary for it. He succeeded Hitler as chancellor for a single day and committed suicide on 1 May 1945 after poisoning his six children.

personas/juan-pablo-ii/resumen.texto: Pope of the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, the first non-Italian since the 16th century. His first trip to Poland, in June 1979, preceded the formation of the Solidarity trade union in 1980, and Gorbachev said that without him the collapse of the Iron Curtain would have been impossible. In 1978 he mediated in the Beagle conflict between Argentina and Chile, and in 2003 he opposed the invasion of Iraq.

personas/jorge-vi/resumen.texto: King of the United Kingdom and the British dominions from 1936 to 1952. He reigned during the Second World War: he stayed in London during the Blitz, when Buckingham Palace was bombed, and became a symbol of British resistance; he was the last Emperor of India, until the dissolution of the Raj in 1947.

personas/hillary-clinton/resumen.texto: First Lady of the United States (1993–2001), senator for New York (2001–2009) and Secretary of State under Barack Obama (2009–2013). As a senator she voted in favor of authorizing the 2002 Iraq War; as Secretary of State she advocated the 2011 military intervention in Libya and was criticized by Republicans for the response to the 2012 attack in Benghazi.

hechos/atentado-de-sarajevo/resumen.texto: On 28 June 1914, the Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip shot dead Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie during an official visit to Sarajevo. The conspirators, from the Young Bosnia organization, had received weapons from the Serbian secret society Black Hand.

hechos/crisis-de-julio/resumen.texto: Chain of diplomatic and military decisions between the Sarajevo assassination and the general war of early August 1914: Germany backed Austria-Hungary with the “blank cheque”, and after the ultimatum to Serbia, mobilizations and alliances drew in Russia, France and the United Kingdom. Responsibility has been debated ever since: Fritz Fischer blamed Germany above all, while authors such as Christopher Clark describe leaders of all the powers who moved forward “like sleepwalkers”.

hechos/austria-hungria-declara-la-guerra.texto: On 28 July 1914, a month after the assassination, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia by telegram, and that night its artillery shelled Belgrade. The three Austro-Hungarian invasions of 1914 failed; Serbia was not occupied until 1915, with the entry of Germany and Bulgaria.

hechos/primera-guerra-mundial/resumen.texto: War between the Allies—France, the Russian Empire, the British Empire, Italy from 1915, the United States from 1917 and others—and the Central Powers—Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria—from 28 July 1914 to the armistice of 11 November 1918. Some nine to ten million soldiers and several million civilians died, and the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires fell.

hechos/invasion-alemana-de-belgica/resum.texto: On 4 August 1914, Germany invaded neutral Belgium to outflank the French army under the Schlieffen Plan, and the United Kingdom declared war on Germany that same night. During the advance, German troops shot some 6,500 Belgian and French civilians and burned the library of the University of Leuven, events that Allied propaganda called “the Rape of Belgium”.

hechos/batalla-de-tannenberg/resumen.texto: Between 26 and 30 August 1914, the German Eighth Army under Hindenburg and Ludendorff encircled and destroyed the Russian Second Army in East Prussia; its commander, Samsonov, took his own life and some 90,000 Russians were taken prisoner.

hechos/primera-batalla-del-marne/resumen.texto: Between 5 and 12 September 1914, the French and British armies halted the German advance some fifty kilometres from Paris and pushed it back to the Aisne. It thwarted the German plan for a short war in the west and gave way to trench warfare.

hechos/tregua-de-navidad/resumen.texto: At Christmas 1914, along several stretches of the Western Front, especially in Flanders, British and German soldiers stopped fighting on their own initiative, left the trenches, exchanged gifts, buried their dead and in some places played football. Commanders prevented it from happening again.

hechos/campana-de-galipoli/resumen.texto: Allied attempt, promoted by Churchill from the Admiralty, to force the Dardanelles and take Constantinople, with landings from 25 April 1915. Ottoman troops, with Mustafa Kemal among their commanders, held out, and the Allies withdrew in January 1916 after more than one hundred thousand deaths on both sides. The day of the landing is a national day in Australia and New Zealand.

hechos/hundimiento-del-lusitania/resumen.texto: On 7 May 1915, a German submarine torpedoed the British ocean liner Lusitania off the south coast of Ireland; nearly 1,200 people died, among them 128 Americans. Outrage in the United States led Germany to restrict submarine warfare for a time.

hechos/batalla-de-verdun/resumen.texto: The longest battle of the war, from 21 February to 18 December 1916: the German army attacked the fortifications of Verdun to bleed the French army white, and the French held out under the slogan “they shall not pass”. It left some 700,000 casualties—dead, wounded and missing—on both sides, including about 300,000 dead, and became a French national symbol.

hechos/batalla-del-somme/resumen.texto: British and French offensive from 1 July to 18 November 1916. On the first day alone the British army suffered more than 57,000 casualties, 19,240 of them killed, the worst day in its history; with more than a million casualties among the three armies, the Allies advanced only a few kilometres. Tanks were used in combat there for the first time.

hechos/batalla-de-jutlandia/resumen.texto: The largest naval battle of the war, on 31 May and 1 June 1916, between the British Grand Fleet and the German High Seas Fleet in the North Sea. The British lost more ships and men, but the German fleet never again challenged them for control of the sea, and Germany turned to submarine warfare.

hechos/entrada-de-estados-unidos-en-la-g.texto: United States enters the First World War

On 6 April 1917, Congress declared war on Germany, which in February had resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and, in the Zimmermann Telegram, had offered Mexico an alliance. By the end of the war some two million American soldiers had reached France.

hechos/batalla-de-passchendaele/resumen.texto: British offensive in Flanders, from July to November 1917, fought on ground turned into a quagmire by rain and artillery. The Allies advanced only a few kilometers at the cost of hundreds of thousands of casualties on both sides, and its name became a byword for the war of attrition.

hechos/paz-de-brest-litovsk/resumen.texto: On March 3, 1918, Bolshevik Russia signed a separate peace with the Central Powers and ceded Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Ukraine. For the Bolsheviks it was the price of consolidating the revolution; for the Allies, a betrayal that prompted their intervention in the Russian Civil War.

hechos/ofensiva-de-los-cien-dias/resumen.texto: Series of Allied offensives launched on August 8, 1918, at Amiens, a day Ludendorff called “the black day of the German Army,” after the failure of the German spring offensive. With tanks, aircraft and fresh American troops, the Allies broke through the Hindenburg Line and drove Germany to seek an armistice.

hechos/armisticio-del-11-de-noviembre/re.texto: Signed in the early hours in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne and in force from eleven in the morning, it ended the fighting on the Western Front. Two days earlier, Wilhelm II had abdicated and a republic had been proclaimed in Germany.

hechos/conferencia-de-paz-de-paris/resum.texto: Meeting of the victors, opened on January 18, 1919, at which Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau and the Italian Vittorio Orlando decided the treaties with the defeated powers: Versailles with Germany, Saint-Germain with Austria, Neuilly with Bulgaria, Trianon with Hungary and Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire. The defeated powers took no part in the negotiations. There the League of Nations was created and the map of Europe and the Middle East was redrawn.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sociedad-de-nacio.texto: Founding of the League of Nations

On January 10, 1920, with the entry into force of the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations came into being, headquartered in Geneva. The United States never joined, Germany did so in 1926 and the USSR in 1934, while Japan, Germany and Italy left it in the 1930s; it was dissolved in 1946 and transferred its assets to the UN.

hechos/incidente-de-mukden/titulo.texto: Mukden Incident and invasion of Manchuria

hechos/incidente-de-mukden/resumen.texto: On September 18, 1931, officers of the Japanese Kwantung Army blew up a section of the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden and blamed the Chinese, as a pretext for occupying Manchuria. In 1932 Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo there, headed by Puyi, the last Qing emperor.

hechos/invasion-italiana-de-etiopia/resu.texto: In October 1935, Mussolini's Italy invaded Ethiopia, a member of the League of Nations, and used poison gas against soldiers and civilians; it took Addis Ababa in May 1936. The League's sanctions excluded oil and failed, and Emperor Haile Selassie's speech in Geneva became a symbol of the impotence of collective security.

hechos/guerra-civil-espanola/resumen.texto: War between the Second Republic and the military officers who rose up in July 1936, led from October by Francisco Franco. The rebels received troops and aircraft from Germany and Italy, and the Republic received Soviet weapons and volunteers from the International Brigades, while the United Kingdom and France promoted non-intervention. It ended on April 1, 1939, with the Francoist victory; estimates of the total death toll, including repression behind the lines on both sides, are around half a million.

hechos/bombardeo-de-guernica/resumen.texto: On April 26, 1937, the German Condor Legion and the Italian air force bombed the Basque town of Guernica in support of the rebels. The Basque government at the time spoke of more than 1,600 dead; recent studies reduce the figure to a few hundred. Picasso made it the subject of his painting Guernica.

hechos/masacre-de-nankin/resumen.texto: After taking Nanjing, then the capital of China, on December 13, 1937, the Japanese army spent weeks murdering prisoners and civilians and raped tens of thousands of women. The Tokyo Tribunal estimated more than 200,000 dead and China cites 300,000, while some Japanese authors give much lower figures or deny it; its memory continues to set the two countries against each other.

hechos/segunda-guerra-sino-japonesa/resu.texto: Open war between China and Japan that began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, near Beijing, on July 7, 1937, and from 1941 merged with the Second World War. Chinese Nationalists and Communists formed an unstable united front; between fifteen and twenty million Chinese died, most of them civilians.

hechos/anschluss/resumen.texto: On March 12, 1938, German troops entered Austria, which was annexed to the Reich the next day; a controlled plebiscite in April gave it more than 99% approval. The persecution of Austrian Jews began immediately.

hechos/conferencia-de-munich/resumen.texto: Hitler, Chamberlain, Daladier and Mussolini agreed on September 29 and 30, 1938, that Czechoslovakia, which had not been invited, should cede the Sudetenland to Germany. Chamberlain promised “peace for our time”; in March 1939 Germany occupied the rest of Bohemia and Moravia.

hechos/noche-de-los-cristales-rotos/resu.texto: Pogrom organized by the Nazi regime on November 9 and 10, 1938, in Germany and Austria, on the pretext of the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a young Jew. Hundreds of synagogues were set on fire and thousands of Jewish businesses looted, at least 91 people were murdered and some 30,000 Jewish men were taken to concentration camps.

hechos/invasion-de-polonia/resumen.texto: Germany attacked Poland on September 1, 1939, after a fake Polish attack staged by the SS at Gleiwitz, and on September 17 the USSR invaded the east of the country under the secret protocol of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact. Warsaw capitulated on September 28 and Poland was partitioned between the two invaders.

hechos/reino-unido-y-francia-declaran-la.texto: The United Kingdom and France declare war on Germany

On September 3, 1939, when their ultimatums expired, the United Kingdom, at eleven in the morning, and France, at five in the afternoon, went to war with Germany to honor their guarantee to Poland; Australia and New Zealand followed that same day, and South Africa and Canada within the following week. They did not attack in the west, and Poland fell within a month.

hechos/guerra-de-invierno/resumen.texto: The USSR invaded Finland on November 30, 1939, and was expelled from the League of Nations. The Finns held out and inflicted heavy Soviet losses, but under the Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940 they had to cede Karelia and other territories, about a tenth of their country.

hechos/masacre-de-katyn/resumen.texto: Between April and May 1940, the Soviet secret police, on the orders of Stalin's Politburo, executed some 22,000 Polish officers, police officers and intellectuals held as prisoners, in the Katyn forest and other sites. The USSR blamed Germany until 1990, when it acknowledged its responsibility.

hechos/evacuacion-de-dunkerque/resumen.texto: Between May 26 and June 4, 1940, surrounded by the German advance, some 338,000 British and French soldiers were evacuated by sea from Dunkirk aboard warships and hundreds of civilian vessels. Churchill called it a “miracle of deliverance” but warned that “wars are not won by evacuations.”

hechos/caida-de-francia/resumen.texto: The German offensive launched on May 10, 1940, through the Ardennes defeated the French, British, Belgian and Dutch armies in six weeks. Paris fell on June 14 and on the 22nd the armistice was signed at Compiègne, in the same railway carriage as in 1918; France was divided between an occupied zone and the collaborationist Vichy regime, headed by Pétain.

hechos/batalla-de-inglaterra/resumen.texto: Air campaign from July to October 1940 in which the Luftwaffe tried to destroy the Royal Air Force as a prelude to an invasion. Its failure led Hitler to postpone the invasion; there followed the bombing of British cities, the Blitz, which killed more than 40,000 civilians up to May 1941.

hechos/operacion-barbarroja/resumen.texto: On June 22, 1941, Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million soldiers, breaking the 1939 pact. After huge advances, the offensive was halted at the gates of Moscow in December. Behind the front, the Einsatzgruppen began the mass murder of Jews: at Babi Yar, near Kyiv, they killed more than 33,000 in two days in September.

hechos/sitio-de-leningrado/resumen.texto: German and Finnish encirclement of Leningrad between September 1941 and January 1944, nearly nine hundred days. Around one million civilians died, most of them from hunger and cold.

hechos/ataque-a-pearl-harbor/resumen.texto: On the morning of December 7, 1941, aircraft from six Japanese aircraft carriers launched a surprise attack on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii: they sank or damaged eight battleships and killed 2,403 Americans. That same day Japan attacked Malaya, the Philippines and Hong Kong, and the next day the United States declared war on it.

hechos/alemania-declara-la-guerra-a-esta.texto: Germany and Italy declare war on the United States

On December 11, 1941, four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler announced war on the United States in the Reichstag and Mussolini did the same in Rome; Congress responded that same day. The European war and the Pacific war became a single world war.

hechos/conferencia-de-wannsee/resumen.texto: Meeting of fifteen senior Nazi officials convened by Heydrich on January 20, 1942, at a villa on the shores of Lake Wannsee, in Berlin, to coordinate among ministries and agencies the deportation and murder of the Jews of Europe, the so-called “Final Solution.” When it met, the mass killings were already under way; the conference organized their extension to the entire continent.

hechos/batalla-de-midway/resumen.texto: Between June 4 and 7, 1942, the US fleet, which had broken the Japanese codes, sank four Japanese aircraft carriers near Midway Atoll, in the central Pacific, and lost one. It marked the end of Japanese expansion in the Pacific.

hechos/segunda-batalla-de-el-alamein/res.texto: Between October 23 and November 11, 1942, Bernard Montgomery's British Eighth Army defeated Erwin Rommel's German-Italian forces in the Egyptian desert and forced them to retreat toward Tunisia. Together with the Allied landings in North Africa, it ended the Axis threat to the Suez Canal.

hechos/batalla-de-stalingrado/resumen.texto: Between August 1942 and February 2, 1943, the German army tried to take the city on the Volga; the Soviet counteroffensive in November encircled Paulus's Sixth Army, which surrendered with some 91,000 survivors. With more than a million military and civilian casualties according to the most conservative estimates, it was one of the bloodiest battles in history and the turning point of the war in the east.

hechos/levantamiento-del-gueto-de-varsov.texto: On April 19, 1943, when the SS began the final deportation from the Warsaw Ghetto, a few hundred Jewish fighters, led by Mordechai Anielewicz, rose up in arms. They held out for nearly a month; on May 16 General Jürgen Stroop declared it over by blowing up the Great Synagogue, and the survivors were murdered or deported to camps.

hechos/batalla-de-kursk/resumen.texto: The last major German offensive in the east, launched on July 5, 1943, against the Kursk salient and stopped by Soviet defenses prepared in advance. It included one of the largest tank battles in history, at Prokhorovka; from then on the initiative on the Eastern Front was Soviet.

hechos/conferencia-de-teheran/resumen.texto: First meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin, from November 28 to December 1, 1943. They agreed to open a second front in France in 1944, and Stalin pledged to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat.

hechos/desembarco-de-normandia/resumen.texto: On June 6, 1944, D-Day, some 156,000 American, British, Canadian and other Allied soldiers landed on five Normandy beaches under Eisenhower's command, in the largest amphibious operation in history. It opened the second front in Western Europe; Paris was liberated on August 25.

hechos/levantamiento-de-varsovia/resumen.texto: Uprising of the Polish Home Army against the German occupation, from August 1 to October 2, 1944, while the Red Army, which had reached the other bank of the Vistula, did not intervene. Some 16,000 Polish fighters and between 150,000 and 200,000 civilians died, and the Germans then razed the city.

hechos/liberacion-de-auschwitz/resumen.texto: On January 27, 1945, Soviet troops entered Auschwitz and found some 7,000 prisoners, most of them sick, whom the SS had left behind when evacuating some 58,000 on “death marches” westward. Since 2005 the date has been the International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

hechos/conferencia-de-yalta/resumen.texto: Meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin at the Livadia Palace, in Crimea, from February 4 to 11, 1945, to decide the postwar order: the occupation of Germany, the fate of Poland, the convening of the UN and Soviet entry into the war against Japan.

hechos/bombardeo-de-dresde/resumen.texto: Between February 13 and 15, 1945, British and American bombers attacked Dresden and caused a firestorm that destroyed the historic center. A commission of historians estimated in 2010 up to 25,000 dead, far below the figures of Nazi propaganda; its military justification remains disputed.

hechos/batalla-de-berlin/resumen.texto: Final Soviet offensive on the German capital, from April 16 to May 2, 1945. Hitler killed himself in his bunker on April 30 and the garrison capitulated on May 2.

hechos/rendicion-de-alemania/resumen.texto: On May 7, 1945, in Reims, and on May 8 in Berlin, the German military chiefs signed the unconditional surrender, which ended the war in Europe. May 8 is celebrated in the West as Victory Day, and May 9 in Russia and other former Soviet countries.

hechos/conferencia-de-san-francisco/resu.texto: Meeting of delegates from fifty countries, from April 25 to June 26, 1945, that drafted and signed the Charter of the United Nations on the basis of the Dumbarton Oaks proposals and what had been agreed at Yalta. The UN formally came into being on October 24, 1945, when the Charter entered into force.

hechos/conferencia-de-potsdam/resumen.texto: Last conference of the three major Allies, from July 17 to August 2, 1945, at the Cecilienhof Palace, with Truman, Stalin and Churchill, who was replaced partway through by Clement Attlee after the latter won the British elections. There Truman informed Stalin that the United States had “a new weapon of unusual destructive force.”

hechos/bombardeos-de-hiroshima-y-nagasak.texto: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

On August 6 and 9, 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the only ones ever used in war; they killed between 150,000 and 246,000 people, most of them civilians. Their defenders argue that they averted an invasion of Japan with far more deaths; their critics, that Japan was close to surrendering and that the Soviet entry into the war, on August 8, weighed as heavily as the bombs. The survivors' organization Nihon Hidankyo received the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize.

hechos/rendicion-de-japon/resumen.texto: Japan announced its acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration on August 15, 1945, and signed the surrender on September 2 aboard the battleship Missouri, in Tokyo Bay, bringing the Second World War to an end. A US occupation followed until 1952.

hechos/segunda-guerra-mundial/resumen.texto: The deadliest war in history, between the Allies—the United Kingdom, France, the Soviet Union, the United States from 1941, China and others—and the Axis—Germany, Italy and Japan—from September 1, 1939, to September 2, 1945. Between 70 and 85 million people died, most of them civilians, among them the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.

hechos/juicios-de-nuremberg/resumen.texto: Trial before the International Military Tribunal, with judges and prosecutors from the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the USSR, of the principal Nazi leaders, from November 20, 1945, to October 1, 1946. It was the first international trial for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity; twelve defendants were sentenced to death.

hechos/juicio-de-tokio/resumen.texto: Tribunal of eleven Allied countries that tried twenty-eight Japanese leaders between May 1946 and November 1948; seven, among them Tojo, were hanged and sixteen were sentenced to life imprisonment. The emperor was not indicted, by decision of the US occupation, and the Indian judge Radhabinod Pal voted to acquit all of them.

hechos/juicio-a-eichmann/resumen.texto: After abducting him in Buenos Aires in May 1960, Israel tried Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem between April and December 1961; the testimony of more than a hundred survivors brought the Holocaust to the attention of a new generation. He was sentenced to death and hanged on June 1, 1962. Argentina protested the abduction before the Security Council, which asked Israel to make reparation.

hechos/particion-de-la-india/resumen.texto: On August 14 and 15, 1947, British India was divided into two independent states, India and Pakistan, the latter with an eastern wing that in 1971 would become Bangladesh, along lines drawn by the Radcliffe Commission. Violence among Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims killed between two hundred thousand and two million people, and between ten and twenty million were displaced, one of the largest forced migrations in history.

hechos/bloqueo-de-berlin/resumen.texto: From June 24, 1948, to May 12, 1949, the USSR cut off land access to the western sectors of Berlin in response to the Allied currency reform. The United States and the United Kingdom supplied two million Berliners through an airlift of more than 270,000 flights. It was the first major crisis of the Cold War and hastened the creation of the two Germanys and of NATO.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-otan/resumen.texto: On April 4, 1949, twelve countries of Western Europe and North America signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, a defensive alliance against the Soviet Union. Its first supreme commander in Europe was Eisenhower, and West Germany joined in 1955.

hechos/guerra-de-corea/resumen.texto: It began on June 25, 1950, with the North's invasion of South Korea. A UN force led by the United States drove the North Koreans back to near the Chinese border, and the intervention of hundreds of thousands of Chinese “volunteers” forced it to retreat. After two years of stalemate near the 38th parallel, the 1953 armistice left the peninsula divided; around three million people died, most of them civilians.

hechos/batalla-de-dien-bien-phu/resumen.texto: Between March and May 1954, General Võ Nguyên Giáp's Viet Minh besieged the French base at Dien Bien Phu, in northwestern Vietnam, and forced its surrender. The defeat led France to accept, at the Geneva Conference, its withdrawal from Indochina and the provisional division of Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

hechos/conferencia-de-bandung/resumen.texto: Meeting of twenty-nine countries of Asia and Africa, most of them newly independent, held in Bandung, Indonesia, in April 1955, with Sukarno, Nehru, Nasser and Zhou Enlai among its leading figures. It condemned colonialism “in all its manifestations” and was the forerunner of the Non-Aligned Movement, founded in 1961.

hechos/guerra-de-argelia/resumen.texto: War of independence launched on November 1, 1954, by the National Liberation Front against French rule. Both sides committed atrocities, including the systematic use of torture by the French army; it ended with the Évian Accords and independence in 1962. Estimates of Algerian deaths range from some 300,000, according to French historians, to one and a half million, the official Algerian figure.

hechos/revolucion-hungara/resumen.texto: Popular uprising that began on October 23, 1956, in Budapest with a student demonstration. Imre Nagy's government announced free elections and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, and on November 4 the Soviet army crushed the revolution; some 2,500 Hungarians died and some 200,000 fled the country.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-cee/titulo.texto: Founding of the European Economic Community

hechos/fundacion-de-la-cee/resumen.texto: On 25 March 1957, six countries signed in Rome the treaties that created the European Economic Community and Euratom, building on the Coal and Steel Community born of the Schuman Declaration. It was the core of today's European Union.

hechos/construccion-del-muro-de-berlin/r.texto: In the early hours of 13 August 1961, the German Democratic Republic closed the border between East and West Berlin with barbed wire, soon replaced by a concrete wall with a guarded strip. Its aim was to stop the flight of East Germans, more than two and a half million of whom had crossed to the West since 1949.

hechos/invasion-de-bahia-de-cochinos/res.texto: On 17 April 1961, some 1,400 Cuban exiles trained and funded by the CIA landed at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow Fidel Castro. They were defeated within three days; the failure drew Cuba even closer to the USSR and preceded the missile crisis.

hechos/crisis-de-los-misiles/resumen.texto: A thirteen-day confrontation in October 1962, after US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy imposed a naval blockade and Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in exchange for a promise not to invade Cuba and, secretly, the removal of US missiles from Turkey. It is the moment when the world came closest to nuclear war; afterwards a direct line was set up between Washington and Moscow.

hechos/incidente-del-golfo-de-tonkin/res.texto: On 2 August 1964, North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked the US destroyer Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin; a second attack, reported on 4 August, never took place, as documents declassified in 2005 confirmed. Johnson ordered retaliatory air strikes and obtained from Congress the resolution that allowed him to escalate the war.

hechos/guerra-de-vietnam/resumen.texto: War between North Vietnam and the Viet Cong, backed by the USSR and China, and South Vietnam, backed by the United States, which had more than half a million soldiers in the country by 1968. It spread to Laos and Cambodia and ended with the fall of Saigon in 1975 and reunification under communist rule. Estimates of Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, range from around one million to more than three million; some 58,000 Americans also died.

hechos/ofensiva-del-tet/resumen.texto: Simultaneous attacks by the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese army on more than a hundred cities in South Vietnam, including the US embassy in Saigon, beginning on 30 January 1968, at the lunar new year. It was a military defeat for the attackers, but it belied official optimism and turned American opinion against the war; in March Johnson gave up seeking re-election.

hechos/masacre-de-my-lai/resumen.texto: On 16 March 1968, US soldiers of Charlie Company killed between 347 and 504 unarmed civilians, mostly women, children and elderly people, in the village of My Lai. The army covered it up until journalist Seymour Hersh revealed it in 1969; only Lieutenant William Calley was convicted, and he served three and a half years of house arrest.

hechos/primavera-de-praga/resumen.texto: Period of reforms that began in January 1968, when Alexander Dubček took over the leadership of the Czechoslovak Communist Party, with freedom of the press, rehabilitation of persecuted people and the project of “socialism with a human face.” On the night of 20–21 August, hundreds of thousands of Warsaw Pact soldiers—Soviet, Bulgarian, Hungarian and some 28,000 Poles from the 2nd Army—invaded the country and ended the reforms; according to documents from Ukrainian archives gathered by Mark Kramer, the firmest supporters of intervention were Andropov, Shelest and Podgorny, while another version attributes the initiative to Gomułka and Ulbricht; East Germany sent no troops, except some specialists, and Romania refused to take part.

hechos/caida-de-saigon/resumen.texto: On 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese tanks entered the presidential palace in Saigon and the government of South Vietnam surrendered, after the helicopter evacuation of the last Americans and thousands of Vietnamese. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

hechos/genocidio-camboyano/resumen.texto: Between 1975 and 1979, Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge regime emptied Cambodia's cities and subjected the population to forced labor in the countryside. Between 1.5 and 2 million people died, close to a quarter of the population, from executions, hunger and disease. The Vietnamese invasion of 1979 overthrew it, and a UN-backed tribunal convicted two of its leaders of genocide in 2018.

hechos/guerra-sovietica-en-afganistan/re.texto: In December 1979, the USSR invaded Afghanistan to prop up the communist government against the Islamist guerrillas, the mujahideen, who received weapons and money from the United States, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and China. The Soviet withdrawal was completed in February 1989, after some 15,000 Soviet soldiers and between half a million and two million Afghans had died, in addition to millions of refugees.

hechos/guerra-iran-irak/resumen.texto: War that began in September 1980 with the Iraqi invasion of Iran ordered by Saddam Hussein, following the Iranian revolution. With attacks on cities, trench warfare and Iraqi chemical weapons, also used against the Kurds of Halabja in 1988, it ended in August 1988 with no border changes and between half a million and a million dead.

hechos/reunificacion-alemana/resumen.texto: On 3 October 1990, less than a year after the fall of the Wall, the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic. It was made possible by the “Two Plus Four” Treaty, signed in September by the two Germanys and the four victorious powers, which renounced their occupation rights.

hechos/guerra-fria/resumen.texto: Global rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies, from the end of the Second World War to the dissolution of the USSR in 1991. The superpowers did not fight each other directly, but they competed in the nuclear and space races and in propaganda, and backed opposing sides in wars such as those in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan.

hechos/guerra-del-golfo/resumen.texto: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990 and annexed it. Once the deadline set by Resolution 678 expired, a coalition of 35 countries led by the United States launched an air campaign on 17 January 1991 and, on 24 February, a ground offensive that drove out the Iraqi troops in a hundred hours. Saddam Hussein remained in power and crushed the Shia and Kurdish uprisings that followed.

hechos/guerras-yugoslavas/resumen.texto: Series of wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia: in Slovenia (1991), Croatia (1991–1995), Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992–1995), Kosovo (1998–1999) and Macedonia (2001). Some 130,000 to 140,000 people died and “ethnic cleansing” displaced millions; the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia tried leaders from all sides.

hechos/sitio-de-sarajevo/resumen.texto: The Bosnian Serb army besieged Sarajevo from April 1992 to February 1996, the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare. Snipers and artillery killed close to 14,000 people, more than 5,000 of them civilians.

hechos/genocidio-de-ruanda/resumen.texto: Between April and July 1994, after the plane carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down, Hutu militias and the Rwandan army killed between 500,000 and 800,000 Tutsis in about a hundred days, according to most estimates (the Rwandan government gives more than a million), as well as opposition Hutus. The UN mission, scaled down after the killing of ten Belgian peacekeepers, did not intervene; it ended with the victory of Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front.

hechos/masacre-de-srebrenica/resumen.texto: In July 1995, after taking the enclave of Srebrenica, declared a “safe area” by the UN and guarded by Dutch peacekeepers, Ratko Mladić's Bosnian Serb forces killed more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys.
