The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice ruled it genocide; the governments of Serbia and Republika Srpska reject that characterization.

hechos/guerra-de-kosovo/resumen.texto: Conflict between Yugoslav forces and the Kosovo Liberation Army, during which some 800,000 Kosovo Albanians were expelled. NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days in 1999 without Security Council authorization, which Russia and China denounced as a violation of international law; it ended with the Serbian withdrawal and a UN administration. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognize.

hechos/segunda-guerra-del-congo/resumen.texto: War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in which nine African countries, among them Rwanda, Uganda, Angola and Zimbabwe, and dozens of militias took part, partly for control of its mineral resources. A study by the International Rescue Committee estimated excess deaths between 1998 and 2007 at 5.4 million, mostly from hunger and disease, a figure other researchers consider exaggerated.

hechos/corte-penal-internacional/resumen.texto: On 1 July 2002 the Rome Statute entered into force and the International Criminal Court began operating in The Hague, the first permanent court to try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The United States, Russia, China and India are not members.

hechos/guerra-de-afganistan/resumen.texto: After 11 September, the United States and its allies attacked the Taliban's Afghanistan, which was sheltering al-Qaeda, on 7 October 2001 and overthrew its government within two months. Twenty years of Taliban insurgency and a NATO mission followed; after the Doha Agreement, the Taliban returned to Kabul on 15 August 2021 and the US withdrawal was completed on the 30th. The Costs of War project estimates some 176,000 deaths in Afghanistan.

hechos/guerra-de-irak/resumen.texto: On 20 March 2003, the United States, the United Kingdom and other allies invaded Iraq without explicit Security Council authorization, claiming that Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction and links to al-Qaeda; Baghdad fell on 9 April and those weapons were never found. An insurgency and a sectarian civil war followed, and US troops withdrew in December 2011. Estimates of Iraqi deaths range from about 150,000 to more than 600,000, depending on the method and period.

hechos/guerra-civil-siria/resumen.texto: It began with the crackdown on the Arab Spring protests in 2011 and became a war between the government of Bashar al-Assad, backed by Russia, Iran and Hezbollah, and rebel groups of various stripes, the Islamic State and Kurdish militias, with intervention by the United States and Turkey. More than half a million people died and more than half the population fled their homes; it ended with the fall of Assad in December 2024.

hechos/anexion-de-crimea/resumen.texto: After the fall of Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych in February 2014, Russian soldiers without insignia seized the peninsula; on 16 March, a referendum held under occupation gave 97% in favor of joining Russia, which annexed it on 18 March. Russia presents it as the self-determination of a mostly Russian population; Ukraine, the UN General Assembly and most states regard it as an illegal annexation.

hechos/guerra-del-donbas/resumen.texto: From April 2014, pro-Russian separatists seized parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk provinces and proclaimed people's republics, with weapons, commanders and, at key moments, regular troops from Russia, which denied its involvement. The Minsk agreements froze the front line without resolving the conflict; between 14,200 and 14,400 people died, among them the 298 aboard flight MH17, shot down in July 2014 by a Russian missile according to the international investigation.

hechos/invasion-rusa-de-ucrania/resumen.texto: Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022 from the north, east and south. It failed to take Kyiv and withdrew from the north in April; Ukraine recaptured Kharkiv and Kherson in late 2022, and Russia proclaimed the annexation of four provinces it only partly occupies. As of November 2026 the war continues with no ceasefire and Russia occupies about a fifth of the country; casualties, killed and wounded, are estimated at between 1.27 and 2 million up to mid-2026, and millions of Ukrainians are displaced or refugees.

hechos/sitio-de-mariupol/resumen.texto: Russian forces encircled the port of Mariupol from late February 2022 and took it in May, after the surrender of the last defenders entrenched in the Azovstal steelworks. Thousands of civilians died, among them those sheltering in the city's theater, bombed in March, and the city was left largely destroyed.

hechos/masacre-de-bucha/resumen.texto: During the Russian occupation of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, in March 2022, hundreds of civilians were killed. Images of bodies in the streets after the Russian withdrawal led to accusations of war crimes and stalled peace negotiations; Russia claims it was staged, which is contradicted by investigations by the UN and the press.

hechos/contraofensiva-de-jarkov/resumen.texto: In September 2022, a lightning Ukrainian offensive recaptured almost all of Kharkiv province, including Izium and Kupiansk, and forced Russian troops to retreat to the Oskil River. Together with the Russian withdrawal from Kherson in November, it was the largest Ukrainian advance of the war.

hechos/orden-de-arresto-contra-putin/tit.texto: International Criminal Court orders Putin's arrest

hechos/orden-de-arresto-contra-putin/res.texto: On 17 March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and the Russian commissioner for children's rights, Maria Lvova-Belova, for the unlawful deportation of children from occupied Ukrainian territories to Russia. Russia does not recognize the Court's jurisdiction and declared the decision null and void.

hechos/incursion-en-kursk/resumen.texto: On 6 August 2024, Ukraine launched the first ground invasion of Russian territory since the Second World War, in Kursk province, and came to control nearly a thousand square kilometers. With the help of North Korean soldiers, Russia retook most of the area by March 2025.

hechos/negociaciones-de-paz-en-ucrania/t.texto: Peace negotiations in the war in Ukraine

hechos/negociaciones-de-paz-en-ucrania/r.texto: Russia and Ukraine negotiated in Belarus and Istanbul in March 2022 without result. Since 2025, Donald Trump's administration has pushed new peace plans, regarded as favorable to Russia and rejected by both sides, and European countries are preparing a “coalition of the willing” to guarantee an eventual ceasefire. Putin demands recognition as Russian of the territories he claims, Ukraine's renunciation of NATO, limits on its army and an end to sanctions; Zelensky calls for an unconditional ceasefire, Russian withdrawal, the return of prisoners and deported children, and security guarantees.

hechos/cumbre-de-alaska/resumen.texto: On 15 August 2025, Donald Trump received Putin at a military base in Anchorage, Alaska, in the first meeting between the two countries' presidents since the 2022 invasion. No agreement on Ukraine was announced, and Trump later suggested that it was up to Ukraine to cede territory.

hechos/guerra-civil-de-sudan/resumen.texto: Since 15 April 2023, the Sudanese army of General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces of General Hemedti have been fighting for control of the country, with backing from various foreign powers. By mid-2026 the war had displaced more than fourteen million people, one of the largest displacement crises in the world.

hechos/periodo-de-entreguerras/resumen.texto: The twenty years and ten months between the armistice of 11 November 1918 and the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939. The Paris Peace Conference redrew the map after the fall of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. It was followed by the “Roaring Twenties,” the Great Depression from 1929, the rise of communism in the USSR and of fascism in Italy and Germany, and colonial independence movements. The powers sought peace through the League of Nations and disarmament pacts; the period ended with the aggressions of Japan, Italy and Germany, the policy of appeasement, and the German–Soviet pact of August 1939.

hechos/guerra-civil-afgana-1989-1992/res.texto: After the Soviet withdrawal (15 February 1989), the mujahideen, who received weapons from the United States and Saudi Arabia through Pakistan, kept fighting the communist government of Najibullah, which had Soviet support until 1991. The offensive on Jalalabad, backed by Pakistan’s intelligence service (ISI), was repulsed between March and June 1989, with about 12,000 to 15,000 civilians killed in that battle alone. Without Soviet aid, and after desertions by the northern militias, which allied with Ahmad Shah Massoud, the government fell in April 1992. The Peshawar Accords proclaimed an interim government, which Hekmatyar rejected, and fighting among the mujahideen for Kabul began on 25 April.

hechos/guerra-civil-afgana-1992-1996/res.texto: Between 28 April 1992 and the Taliban’s capture of Kabul on 27 September 1996, the mujahideen factions fought for the capital in shifting alliances. According to Human Rights Watch, almost all of them (the Jamiat of Rabbani and Massoud, Junbish, Wahdat, Hezb-e Islami and Ittehad) contributed to destroying a third of Kabul and killing thousands of civilians; between January and June 1994 alone, 25,000 people died in the city. In the Afshar massacre (February 1993), government forces under Rabbani and Sayyaf’s Ittehad killed Hazara civilians. The Taliban, who had emerged with Pakistani support, took Kandahar in 1994, Herat in 1995 and Kabul in 1996.

hechos/guerra-civil-afgana-1996-2001/res.texto: From the Taliban’s capture of Kabul (27 September 1996), when they proclaimed the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, until the US invasion on 7 October 2001. Only Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates recognized the Emirate. Massoud formed the United Front (Northern Alliance), backed by Iran, India, Russia, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkey, while the Taliban had military support from Pakistan, Saudi money and al-Qaeda fighters. In May 1997 they entered Mazar-i-Sharif after Malik switched sides, were expelled days later, and some 3,000 Taliban prisoners were executed. They took the city in August 1998, with the killing of thousands of Hazaras.

hechos/guerra-de-indochina/resumen.texto: War between France, with the State of Vietnam of Bảo Đại, and the Viet Minh of Ho Chi Minh, who had proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1945. Open war began on 19 December 1946, after the French bombardment of Haiphong on 23 November (about 6,000 civilians killed). After the Communist victory in China in 1949, China gave the Viet Minh doctrine, training and advisers, and the USSR provided war materiel, while the United States helped France. The French defeat at Dien Bien Phu (1954) led to the Geneva Conference, which divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel. Between 400,000 and 842,707 soldiers and between 125,000 and 400,000 civilians died, and both sides committed war crimes.

hechos/guerra-civil-griega/resumen.texto: War between the government of the Kingdom of Greece and the Democratic Army of Greece (DSE), the armed wing of the Communist Party (KKE), which proclaimed a provisional government backed by Albania and Yugoslavia. Fighting resumed in March 1946, after the resistance had split and after the fighting in Athens in 1944. The government received aid from the United Kingdom and, from the Truman Doctrine of 1947, from the United States, which is why it is considered the first indirect conflict of the Cold War; on 16 October 1949 the KKE announced a “temporary ceasefire.” Massacres were committed on both sides, and nearly 100,000 DSE fighters and sympathizers were imprisoned, exiled or executed. About 30,000 children went to countries of the Eastern Bloc (the UN commission found that some were taken by force; the KKE spoke of evacuation at the request of parents), and the government housed more than 25,000 in “children’s towns.”

hechos/golpe-de-estado-en-iran-de-1953/r.texto: Between 15 and 19 August 1953, a coup organized by British (MI6, “Operation Boot”) and American (CIA, “Operation Ajax”) services overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, who had nationalized oil in 1951 against the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Mosaddegh dissolved parliament with a referendum in August (99.9%, boycotted and described as fraudulent). The shah decreed his dismissal and appointed Zahedi; between 200 and 300 people died. Mosaddegh was convicted of treason on 21 December and sentenced to three years in prison, and he remained under house arrest until his death in 1967. In 2013 the United States declassified documents acknowledging its role. Ray Takeyh (2014) argues that the CIA’s attempt failed and that Iranian forces decided the outcome on 19 August, and Alvandi and Gasiorowski (2019) call this a highly biased reading of the evidence.

hechos/guerra-sino-india/resumen.texto: Border conflict between China and India from 20 October to 21 November 1962, in the North-East Frontier Agency (now Arunachal Pradesh) and in Aksai Chin. China did not recognize the Johnson and McMahon lines, which India accepted, and tensions grew after the Tibetan uprising of 1959, when India gave asylum to the Dalai Lama. In 1961–1962 India pursued a “forward policy” (some 60 posts in the disputed zone, with permission to open fire from July 1962). China presented its offensive as a response (as Maxwell and Whiting read it), while for India it was Chinese aggression. Chinese troops broke the Indian positions and reached near Tezpur. China declared a unilateral ceasefire, withdrew 20 km behind the line of 7 November 1959, and kept Aksai Chin.

hechos/guerra-de-liberacion-de-banglades.texto: After the Awami League won 167 of the 169 seats of East Pakistan in 1970 (a majority in the National Assembly) and the political standoff that followed, the Pakistani army launched “Operation Searchlight” against the Bengali population on 25 March 1971. The Mukti Bahini, trained by the Indian army, began a guerrilla war, and border fighting broke out before India entered the war on 3 December. About ten million refugees fled to India, and Pakistan surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December. The army and its militias committed mass killings and rapes (from 300,000 to 3 million dead according to Bangladeshi sources, from 125,000 to 505,000 according to independent researchers), and it has been described as genocide. There was also violence by Bengali nationalists against Biharis (Rummel estimates 150,000 dead; Bihari representatives spoke of 500,000). The USSR supported India (treaty of August 1971 and vetoes at the UN); China and the United States, with Nixon, backed Pakistan.

hechos/ruptura-sino-sovietica/resumen.texto: Gradual deterioration of relations between the People’s Republic of China and the USSR. In 1956 Khrushchev denounced Stalin, and Mao rejected de-Stalinization as “revisionism.” In June 1960, at the meeting of communist parties in Bucharest, Khrushchev clashed with Peng Zhen, head of the Chinese delegation; the USSR withdrew some 1,400 technicians that year, and in 1961 Beijing denounced the Soviets as “revisionist traitors.” The rivalry for leadership of communism led to armed clashes on the border in 1969 (Zhenbao Island), after which, according to Chinese and US sources, the USSR considered a nuclear attack. For the West it changed the Cold War and facilitated Nixon’s trip to China in 1972.

hechos/revoluciones-de-1989/resumen.texto: A wave of movements that toppled most of the Marxist-Leninist governments of the Eastern Bloc. It began with Solidarity in Poland, whose partly free elections of 4 June 1989 confirmed its victory; it was followed by the opening of the Hungarian border with Austria, the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November, and the revolutions in Czechoslovakia and Bulgaria. In Romania the regime fell by force: Ceaușescu was executed on 25 December. Except in Romania, civil resistance predominated. In China the Tiananmen protests ended with military repression on 4 June, and the Communist Party kept power. These events accelerated the dissolution of the USSR and the end of the Cold War.

hechos/batalla-de-moscu/resumen.texto: A campaign of the Second World War on a 600-km front, from the German “Operation Typhoon” of 30 September 1941 to 7 January 1942 (some authors extend it to April, with the Rzhev offensive). The Soviets raised three defensive belts, brought in troops from Siberia and the Far East, and halted the German advance in early December; the counteroffensive of 5 December pushed the Germans back between 100 and 250 km. It ended German hopes of a quick victory, and Hitler dismissed the army commander, Brauchitsch, on 19 December. Casualty figures differ: Erickson counts 653,924 Soviet casualties through January; Bellamy, 926,224 irrecoverable losses through April; the official reports of Army Group Center record 35,757 German dead, 128,716 wounded and 9,721 missing, figures that other researchers consider underestimated.

hechos/operacion-bagration/resumen.texto: Soviet offensive in Belarus between 22 June and 19 August 1944, shortly after the Normandy landings. Using deception (maskirovka) and concentrated forces, the Red Army destroyed Army Group Center (28 divisions), the greatest defeat in German military history. It took Minsk in early July and reached the Vistula and the outskirts of Warsaw, where it halted while the Germans crushed the uprising; its role remains disputed among historians. German losses are estimated at 400,000 to 540,000 killed, missing and wounded; Soviet losses at 180,040 killed and missing and 590,848 wounded and sick.

hechos/rebelion-del-grupo-wagner/resumen.texto: On 23 June 2023, after six months of conflict with the Ministry of Defense, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner Group rose up against the Russian government. Prigozhin accused Shoigu and Gerasimov of the military failures in Ukraine and of having attacked his men, which the Russian government denied. The mercenaries occupied Rostov-on-Don and an armored column advanced toward Moscow; Putin spoke of treason. Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko mediated an agreement; Prigozhin halted the march on 24 June, and on 27 June the charges against the Wagner fighters were dropped. At least thirteen Russian servicemen were killed. Prigozhin died on 23 August 2023 in the explosion of his plane.

hechos/conferencia-de-casablanca/resumen.texto: Meeting of Roosevelt and Churchill at the Anfa Hotel in Casablanca, in French-protectorate Morocco, from 14 to 24 January 1943. Stalin, who had been invited, did not attend because of the Battle of Stalingrad; De Gaulle and Giraud attended without taking part in military planning. It was agreed to invade Sicily before France, to intensify the strategic bombing of Germany and to demand the “unconditional surrender” of the Axis; according to the journalist Drew Middleton, who was in Casablanca, Churchill was surprised to hear it announced in public, and the diplomat Charles Bohlen attributes the doctrine almost entirely to Roosevelt.

hechos/transformacion-de-la-csce-en-osce.texto: On 1 January 1995, as decided at the 1994 Budapest conference, the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, born from the Helsinki Final Act as a forum for dialogue between the two blocs, was renamed the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, with a permanent secretariat in Vienna. It observes elections and monitors human rights and arms control; its mandate in Ukraine expired on 31 March 2022 because of Russian objections.

hechos/invasion-de-irak-de-2003/resumen.texto: First phase of the Iraq War. It began on 20 March 2003 with an air strike on the presidential palace in Baghdad, and a coalition of troops, mostly American, British, Australian and Polish, occupied the country; Baghdad fell on 9 April and on 1 May Bush declared the end of “major combat operations.” Washington and London invoked weapons of mass destruction, whose existence the UN inspectors had not verified; the Iraq Survey Group (Duelfer Report, 2004) did not find the weapons of mass destruction stockpiles that had been invoked, only small quantities of chemical weapons, insufficient for a significant military threat; Canada, France and Germany opposed it, and Kofi Annan called the invasion illegal in 2004.

hechos/batalla-de-dunkerque/resumen.texto: Between 26 May and 4 June 1940, while the Allied armies were being evacuated, their rearguard, mostly French, defended the Dunkirk perimeter against the German advance and the Luftwaffe; the bombing killed more than a thousand civilians in the town. On 24 May the German tanks were halted by a “halt order” whose reason is still debated: it was proposed by Rundstedt and Kluge and sanctioned by Hitler. The Germans captured some 35,000 soldiers, almost all French, who covered the embarkation.

hechos/primera-guerra-chechena/resumen.texto: War between Russia and the separatist republic of Chechnya, governed by Dzhokhar Dudayev from 1991. On 11 December 1994 Yeltsin sent some 40,000 soldiers; Grozny fell in March 1995 after bombing and urban combat that killed thousands of civilians, but the Russians did not control the rest of the territory. After the separatists retook Grozny in August 1996, the Khasavyurt Accord ended hostilities. Between 30,000 and 100,000 Chechen civilians died; Russia acknowledged 5,500 military deaths, and independent estimates range from 5,000 to 14,000.

hechos/segunda-guerra-chechena/resumen.texto: It began in August 1999 with the entry of Chechen Islamists into Dagestan and bombings of apartment buildings in Russia, which killed more than 300 people and which the government attributed to Chechens; Prime Minister Putin ordered the invasion on 1 October. Russia took Grozny on 2 February 2000 after a siege that devastated it, imposed direct rule and declared the “counter-terrorist operation” over on 16 April 2009. The official Russian investigation attributed the bombings to Achemez Gochiyayev. On 22 September 1999 Ryazan police caught FSB agents placing a bomb in an apartment building; Moscow ordered their release, and the FSB chief, Nikolai Patrushev, called it a “training exercise.” Deputies Kovalev, Shchekochikhin and Yushenkov doubted that version, and critics such as Litvinenko and Felshtinsky argue that the bombings were an FSB operation, a thesis contrary to the official one. Both sides attacked civilians; there is no certain death toll, with estimates from about 25,000 to more than 60,000, mostly Chechen civilians.

hechos/guerra-ruso-ucraniana/resumen.texto: War between Russia and Ukraine, ongoing since February 2014. After the Euromaidan and the flight of President Yanukovych, unmarked Russian troops occupied Crimea, which Russia annexed in March after a referendum held under occupation; Moscow called what happened in Kyiv a “coup d’état.” In April, Russian-backed separatist groups took cities in the Donbas and proclaimed the Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics. The Minsk II agreements of 2015 were not fully implemented, and on 24 February 2022 Russia launched the full-scale invasion.

hechos/batalla-de-las-ardenas/resumen.texto: Last major German offensive on the Western Front, from 16 December 1944 to 25 January 1945, through the Belgian and Luxembourgish Ardennes; it aimed to take the port of Antwerp and split the Allied lines. It achieved complete surprise, but American resistance at Elsenborn and at Bastogne, which was encircled until Patton's Third Army arrived on 26 December, halted it. On 17 December, near Malmedy, SS troops killed some 84 American prisoners. German losses were between 63,000 and 104,000 men killed, wounded and missing; the figures for American casualties do not agree, ranging from about 77,000 to 89,000, with between 8,600 and 19,000 dead.

hechos/guerra-de-broma/resumen.texto: Period between the British and French declarations of war on Germany, on 3 September 1939, and the German invasion of France and the Netherlands on 10 May 1940, during which the Western Allies barely undertook ground operations despite their commitment to Poland. The French offensive in the Saar of 7 September 1939 held back only six German divisions and was abandoned in October; the Allies did impose a naval blockade and discussed intervening in Norway, in the Balkans and to aid Finland. It is also known as “drôle de guerre” and “Sitzkrieg.”

hechos/batalla-de-normandia/resumen.texto: Allied campaign, codenamed Overlord, which began with the landings of 6 June 1944 and ended on 30 August with the German retreat beyond the Seine. The Allies took Cherbourg on 26 June and Caen on 21 July, and trapped some 50,000 German soldiers in the Falaise pocket; more than two million men had landed in northern France by 21 August. It cost the US Army 124,394 casualties (20,668 dead) and the British and Canadian armies 83,045; German losses are estimated at about 210,000 according to Niklas Zetterling and between 400,000 and 530,000 according to other sources, with 233,000 prisoners taken from June to August according to Allied reports. Between 13,632 and 19,890 French civilians died, to which another 11,000 to 19,000 dead from the earlier bombings must be added.

hechos/firma-de-la-orden-ejecutiva-9066/.texto: Executive Order 9066 and the internment of Japanese Americans

On 19 February 1942, two months after Pearl Harbor, Roosevelt signed the order that allowed the exclusion of any person from military zones; it was used to expel some 125,000 people of Japanese descent, two-thirds of them American citizens, from the West Coast and confine them in relocation camps. In 1944 the Supreme Court upheld the exclusion in Korematsu v. United States (6 votes to 3); in 1976 Ford formally ended the order; in 1982 a congressional commission concluded that the confinement was due to “racial prejudice, war hysteria and a failure of political leadership,” and the 1988 law provided for an apology and $20,000 to each surviving internee.

hechos/guerra-polaco-sovietica/resumen.texto: War between the Second Polish Republic and Soviet Russia, from 14 February 1919 to 18 March 1921. Polish leaders, with Piłsudski, sought to restore the borders that existed before 1772, and Lenin saw Poland as the path to carrying the revolution into Europe. In April 1920, with Ukrainian allies of Petliura, Piłsudski launched an offensive that took Kyiv on 7 May; the Red Army counterattacked from June and reached Warsaw in August, where it was defeated. The Treaty of Riga divided the disputed territories and fixed the Polish border some 200 km east of the Curzon Line, with part of Ukraine and Belarus under Polish rule; Piłsudski's project of a federation led by Poland failed.

hechos/batalla-de-varsovia-1920/resumen.texto: Around mid-August 1920 Tukhachevsky's Red Army reached the gates of Warsaw; Piłsudski's Polish counterattack from the south, on 16 August, forced it to retreat in disorder until 25 August. Poles call it “the Miracle on the Vistula.” Estimated Russian losses were 10,000 dead, 30,000 wounded and 66,000 prisoners, against about 4,500 Polish dead. It ended the Soviet offensive toward the west.

hechos/evacuacion-de-crimea-de-1920/resu.texto: Between 13 and 16 November 1920, after the Red Army broke through the Perekop line, General Wrangel evacuated by sea between 145,000 and 150,000 soldiers and civilians from Sevastopol, Yevpatoria, Kerch, Feodosia and Yalta. It marked the end of the last White stronghold and of the fighting on the southern front of the Russian Civil War. Those who stayed behind suffered a wave of repression with mass executions, estimated at between 12,000 and 120,000, although an amnesty had been promised to those who surrendered.

hechos/pacto-balcanico-de-1934/resumen.texto: On 9 February 1934 Greece, Romania, Turkey and Yugoslavia signed the Balkan Entente in Athens to maintain the territorial status quo of the postwar period and present a common front against Bulgaria's claims. Italy, Albania, Bulgaria, Hungary and the Soviet Union refused to sign it. The Second World War rendered it ineffective.

hechos/asesinato-de-alejandro-i-de-yugos.texto: Assassination of Alexander I of Yugoslavia

On 9 October 1934, during an official visit to France, King Alexander I of Yugoslavia was shot in Marseille by Vlado Chernozemski of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization (IMRO), with support from Ante Pavelić's Ustaše; French Foreign Minister Louis Barthou was also killed. He was succeeded by his eleven-year-old son Peter II, under a regency headed by Prince Paul.

hechos/invasion-italiana-de-albania/resu.texto: From 7 to 12 April 1939, after an ultimatum of 25 March, Italy invaded Albania with a force that totalled 100,000 men, of whom some 22,000 landed. The Albanian army, of some 15,000 poorly equipped soldiers, resisted mainly at Durrës; King Zog fled to Greece and the country became a protectorate in personal union with the Italian crown.

hechos/disolucion-del-territorio-libre-d.texto: Dissolution of the Free Territory of Trieste

The Free Territory of Trieste, created in 1947 by the peace treaty with Italy, was de facto dissolved in 1954: a memorandum signed in London gave Italy civil administration of Zone A, including the city of Trieste, and Yugoslavia that of Zone B. The border remained disputed until the Treaty of Osimo in 1975.

hechos/ruptura-albano-sovietica/resumen.texto: Deterioration of relations between the USSR and Albania from 1956, following Khrushchev's rapprochement with Yugoslavia, the “secret speech” and de-Stalinization, which Enver Hoxha regarded as revisionism. It became public in 1960, when the Albanian delegation did not support Khrushchev against China at the Bucharest conference, and ended in the severing of relations in 1961, in the context of the Sino-Soviet split. Albania withdrew from the Warsaw Pact in 1968, in reaction to the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

hechos/tratado-de-osimo/resumen.texto: On 10 November 1975 Italy and Yugoslavia signed the treaty at Osimo that definitively divided the Free Territory of Trieste: the city of Trieste and its coastal strip (Zone A) went to Italy, and northwest Istria (Zone B) to Yugoslavia. It entered into force on 11 October 1977; in Italy it was heavily criticized for the secrecy of the negotiations and for the cession of Istria.

hechos/discurso-de-gazimestan/resumen.texto: On 28 June 1989, before an audience estimated at one million or more, Slobodan Milošević spoke at the Gazimestan monument on the Kosovo field, on the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo, months after reducing the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina (in March there had been Albanian deaths in protests). He said that Serbia faced “battles” that “are not armed, although such things still cannot be ruled out.” The British journalist Marcus Tanner, who attended, wrote that Serbian nationalist fervor had perhaps permanently destroyed any possibility of agreement on Kosovo; Tim Judah conjectured that Milošević spoke of “armed battles” to intimidate the other Yugoslav leaders; Milan Milošević (no relation) said he was thinking of Kosovo and not of the wars that followed; and Slobodan Milošević argued before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, in 2002 and 2005, that it was a speech of peace.

hechos/transferencia-de-crimea-a-ucrania.texto: On 19 February 1954 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR transferred Crimea Oblast from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR; the Politburo had approved it on 25 January, according to documents in the Russian State Archive. It was presented as a tribute to the tercentenary of the Treaty of Pereiaslav and is attributed to Khrushchev. Its legality is disputed: the Supreme Soviet of Russia questioned it in 1992, and the Russian Prosecutor General's Office said in 2015 that it violated the Soviet Constitution, while Mark Kramer holds that the minutes show the consent of the parliaments of both republics.

hechos/operacion-anadyr/resumen.texto: Secret Soviet deployment to Cuba in 1962: R-12 and R-14 ballistic missiles, medium-range bombers, cruise missiles with tactical nuclear warheads, and a mechanized infantry division, with 50,874 personnel according to the plan approved by Malinovsky on 4 July and by Khrushchev three days later. Between June and mid-October, 86 ships made 180 voyages from Baltiysk, Liepāja, Sevastopol, Feodosia, Nikolayev, Poti, Murmansk and Kronstadt; the code name, that of a river and a city in the Russian Far East, was meant to mislead American intelligence. Its discovery sparked the missile crisis.

hechos/grupo-helsinki-de-ucrania/resumen.texto: Founded on 9 November 1976 as the “Ukrainian Public Group to Promote the Implementation of the Helsinki Accords,” to monitor human rights in Ukraine, relying on Principle VII of the Final Act. From February 1977 Soviet authorities arrested its members: within two years all the founders had been sentenced to between 7 and 10 years in prison or exile; by the end of 1979 six had been forced to emigrate and several had been subjected to psychiatric confinement; by 1981 all were in prison.

hechos/incidente-del-mar-negro-de-1988/r.texto: On 12 February 1988 the Soviet frigates Bezzavetny and SKR-6 brushed against the US cruiser USS Yorktown and the destroyer USS Caron, which were exercising “innocent passage” through Soviet territorial waters off Crimea. The USSR allowed such passage only through designated sea corridors; the United States, which saw no legal basis for that restriction, had since 1979 run a freedom-of-navigation exercise program. There was minor damage, and after the incident Moscow agreed to resolve the matter.

hechos/cumbre-de-la-otan-en-bucarest-de-.texto: From 2 to 4 April 2008 NATO invited Croatia and Albania to join, but not Macedonia, because of its dispute with Greece over the name. Georgia and Ukraine asked for a Membership Action Plan and did not receive one, chiefly because of opposition from Germany and France (the United States, Canada, Poland, Romania and the Baltic states supported it), but the declaration said that “these countries will become members of NATO” and that their request would be reviewed in December. Putin attended on the second day and opposed the missile shield in Poland and the Czech Republic.

hechos/protestas-de-poznan-de-1956/resum.texto: From 28 to 30 June 1956, workers at the Cegielski factory who were demanding better conditions were repressed by some 10,000 soldiers and 400 tanks when some 100,000 people gathered in front of the headquarters of Public Security. The historian Łukasz Jastrząb of the Institute of National Remembrance estimates 57 dead and hundreds wounded; other estimates exceed one hundred dead. The first of the major protests against the Polish communist government, it was a milestone on the way to “Polish October” and to a government less subordinated to Moscow.

hechos/tratado-de-varsovia-de-1970/resum.texto: On 7 December 1970 Chancellor Willy Brandt and Prime Minister Józef Cyrankiewicz signed in Warsaw the treaty between the Federal Republic of Germany and Poland, part of Ostpolitik: both renounced the use of force, and the FRG accepted the Oder–Neisse line as Poland's western border. The Christian Democratic opposition (CDU/CSU) described it as a betrayal of national interests; the Bundestag ratified it on 17 May 1972, and reunified Germany reaffirmed the border in the treaty of 14 November 1990.

hechos/conferencia-de-bonn-sobre-afganis.texto: International Conference on Afghanistan in Bonn

On 5 December 2011, at the Petersberg Hotel in Bonn, delegations from 85 states, 15 international organizations and the UN met at the request of President Karzai, ten years after the 2001 Bonn conference. They discussed the transfer of security to the Afghan government planned for 2014, the international role afterwards and political stabilization, and concluded with a declaration of international support for another decade. Pakistan boycotted the conference following the NATO attack on its territory.

hechos/acuerdo-de-nassau/resumen.texto: Agreement negotiated in the Bahamas between Kennedy and Macmillan, concluded on 21 December 1962, to resolve the Skybolt crisis: the air-to-surface missile that the United States had cancelled and on which Britain's independent nuclear deterrent depended. Washington agreed to supply submarine-launched Polaris missiles, which the United Kingdom would assign to NATO in a multilateral force and could use on its own only when “supreme national interests” were at stake. It was the basis of the Polaris Sales Agreement of 6 April 1963.

hechos/declaracion-conjunta-sino-britani.texto: On 19 December 1984 Thatcher and Premier Zhao Ziyang signed in Beijing the treaty by which the United Kingdom would return Hong Kong to China on 1 July 1997, the date on which the lease of the New Territories expired. China undertook to establish a special administrative region with a high degree of autonomy, except in defence and foreign affairs (“one country, two systems”), and to maintain that policy for 50 years. It entered into force on 27 May 1985. Since 2014 China has maintained that the treaty is exhausted and has no legal effect; the United Kingdom maintains that it remains in force.

hechos/tratado-del-eliseo/resumen.texto: Treaty of friendship between France and West Germany, signed on 22 January 1963 at the Élysée Palace by De Gaulle and Adenauer. It established regular consultations on defence, education and youth, with summits of heads of state and government at least twice a year and meetings of foreign ministers every three months, and provided an institutional basis for ending the enmity between the two countries.

hechos/cumbre-de-rambouillet-de-1975/res.texto: From 15 to 17 November 1975, at the Château de Rambouillet, the president of France and the chancellor of West Germany brought together the heads of government of France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States in an informal forum, the G6, in the face of the worst recession since the 1930s. It was the origin of the annual summits that would become the G7 and G8.

hechos/acuerdo-nuclear-con-iran-de-2015/.texto: On 14 July 2015, after twenty months of negotiation, Iran, the P5+1 (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, plus Germany) and the European Union agreed in Vienna to limit Iran's nuclear programme (centrifuges, enrichment and uranium stockpiles, with more IAEA inspections) in exchange for easing the nuclear sanctions of the UN, the EU and the United States. It entered into force on 20 January 2016; Israel, Saudi Arabia and the US Republican Party criticized it. The United States withdrew in 2018, under Donald Trump, and imposed new sanctions.

hechos/guerras-de-los-balcanes/resumen.texto: In the first war (8 October 1912 to 30 May 1913), Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro, united in the Balkan League, defeated the Ottoman Empire, which lost almost all its European territories except eastern Thrace; the Treaty of London included the independence of Albania. In the second (from 29 June 1913), Bulgaria attacked its former allies, was defeated by Serbia and Greece, and was also attacked by Romania and the Ottoman Empire, which recovered Adrianople (Edirne); the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) divided Macedonia. All sides committed atrocities against civilians and ethnic cleansing; the enlargement of Serbia and the relative weakening of Austria-Hungary are part of the background to the July Crisis of 1914.

hechos/frente-oriental-de-la-segunda-gue.texto: Eastern Front of World War II

Theatre of the Second World War between Nazi Germany, its allies and Finland on one side, and the Soviet Union on the other, from the German invasion of 22 June 1941 to Germany's surrender in May 1945 (8 May in Western Europe, 9 May in the USSR). It included Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk and Operation Bagration, and was the largest military confrontation in history; estimates of deaths, civilians included, are around 30 million. Germany waged a war of annihilation, with famine, mass deportations and massacres, and Stalin ordered his army in retreat to apply the scorched-earth policy.

hechos/holodomor/resumen.texto: Famine in Soviet Ukraine (and in other areas, such as the Kuban) during collectivization and the high grain quotas. Among the measures of those months were the Law of Spikelets (7 August 1932), the blacklists of villages (20 November), internal passports (27 December) and the secret directive of 22 January 1933, signed by Stalin, which banned peasants in Ukraine and the Kuban from leaving; grain exports continued (1.8 million tonnes in 1932–1933, according to Michael Ellman), and the government denied the famine and did not seek foreign aid. Snyder cites 2.4 million excess deaths on record (a figure he considers low); recent studies give between 3.5 and 5 million, and a 2003 statement by 25 countries at the UN spoke of 7 to 10 million, a figure that Snyder and Wheatcroft criticize. It is debated whether it was deliberate, whether it targeted Ukrainians and whether it was genocide: Anne Applebaum argues that the deaths were due to the requisitions and that for this reason they were intentional, and Snyder points to lethal policies limited to Ukraine, while R. W. Davies and Wheatcroft attribute it chiefly to Stalin's economic policy and say that speaking of a “man-made” famine underestimates the natural causes, and Mark Tauger stresses the poor harvest; there is no document explicitly ordering the starvation of a region. Ukraine, 33 other states and the European Parliament recognize it as genocide, and the Russian Duma in 2008 condemned the Soviet regime without using that word.

hechos/tratado-de-lausana/resumen.texto: After the Turkish victory in the Greco-Turkish War and the Armistice of Mudanya (October 1922), İsmet İnönü, Lord Curzon and Eleftherios Venizelos negotiated peace at the conference opened on 20 November 1922. The treaty, signed on 24 July 1923, replaced the Treaty of Sèvres, recognized the Republic of Turkey and fixed its borders with Greece and Bulgaria; most of Turkey's Christian population and Greece's Muslim population had already been deported under a prior exchange convention. Its Declaration of Amnesty granted immunity for acts committed from 1914 to 1922, and the historian Hans-Lukas Kieser argues that with it the treaty tacitly endorsed the expulsions and extermination, including the Armenian genocide.

hechos/convencion-sobre-los-derechos-del.texto: Convention on the Rights of the Child

The UN General Assembly adopted it and opened it for signature on 20 November 1989; it entered into force on 2 September 1990. It defines a child as any person under 18 years of age, unless national law sets the age of majority earlier. There are 196 States Parties, including all UN members except the United States; an Optional Protocol of 2000 restricts the recruitment of minors in armed conflicts.

hechos/pacto-internacional-de-derechos-c.texto: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights

The UN General Assembly adopted it on 16 December 1966 (resolution 2200 A) and it entered into force on 23 March 1976. It obliges States to respect rights such as life, freedom of expression, of religion and of assembly, electoral rights and guarantees of a fair trial; together with the Universal Declaration and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, it forms the International Bill of Human Rights. It has 175 States parties (as of December 2025); China and Cuba signed it without ratifying it.

hechos/acuerdo-de-schengen/resumen.texto: Signed on 14 June 1985 near Schengen, in Luxembourg, by five of the ten members of the European Economic Community (Belgium, France, West Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands), it proposed the gradual abolition of controls at common borders. The 1990 Convention envisaged the removal of systematic internal controls and a common visa policy, and has been in force since 1995. The Treaty of Amsterdam incorporated it into European Union law in 1999; the Schengen Area now comprises 29 European countries.

lugares/sede-de-la-onu/resumen.texto: Complex on the banks of the East River, in Manhattan, built between 1948 and 1952 on land donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr., designed by an international team led by Wallace Harrison that included Le Corbusier and Oscar Niemeyer. The General Assembly and the Security Council meet there.

lugares/hiroshima/resumen.texto: Port city in western Japan founded in 1589 next to the castle of Mōri Terumoto, seat of an important military command during the Second World War. On 6 August 1945 it became the first city attacked with an atomic bomb; the Atomic Bomb Dome and the Peace Memorial Park commemorate the victims.

lugares/auschwitz/resumen.texto: Complex of concentration and extermination camps that Nazi Germany built from 1940 next to Oświęcim, in occupied Poland. Around 1.1 million people were murdered there, the vast majority of them Jews, almost all in the gas chambers of Birkenau. Liberated by the Red Army on 27 January 1945, it is now a museum and a World Heritage Site.

lugares/palacio-de-versalles/resumen.texto: Hunting lodge of Louis XIII turned by Louis XIV, from 1661, into the residence of the French court. In its Hall of Mirrors the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 and peace with Germany was signed on 28 June 1919.

lugares/pearl-harbor/resumen.texto: Lagoon on the island of Oahu, in Hawaii, where the United States established from 1908 the main naval base of its Pacific Fleet. The Japanese attack of 7 December 1941 sank or damaged eight battleships and killed 2,403 Americans; the USS Arizona Memorial stands over the battleship's sunken hull.

lugares/palacio-de-justicia-de-nuremberg.texto: Courthouse completed in 1916 that the Allies chose for the International Military Tribunal because it was almost intact and had an adjoining prison. In its Courtroom 600 the leading Nazi officials were tried in 1945 and 1946, followed by other defendants in the twelve subsequent American trials; it now houses a museum.

lugares/puerta-de-brandeburgo/resumen.texto: Neoclassical gateway in Berlin completed in 1791. Between 1961 and 1989 it stood in the border strip between East and West Berlin and was the symbol of Germany's division; in 1987 Reagan delivered in front of it his call to tear down the wall.

lugares/muro-de-berlin/resumen.texto: Barrier of concrete and wire, with watchtowers and a death strip, that the German Democratic Republic built from 13 August 1961 around West Berlin. At least 140 people died trying to cross it; it was opened on 9 November 1989 and some sections remain as memorials.

lugares/checkpoint-charlie/resumen.texto: Border crossing on Friedrichstrasse between the American and Soviet sectors of Berlin, reserved for foreigners and Allied personnel. In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other there for sixteen hours; it was dismantled in 1990.

lugares/playa-de-omaha/resumen.texto: Sector of the Normandy coast where American troops landed on 6 June 1944, D-Day, and where the attackers suffered the heaviest casualties of the day. On the bluff above stands the American cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer.

lugares/palacio-de-la-paz/resumen.texto: Building in The Hague inaugurated in 1913 with funds from Andrew Carnegie for the Permanent Court of Arbitration created at the 1899 peace conference. Since 1946 it has also been the seat of the International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the UN.

lugares/palacio-de-las-naciones/resumen.texto: Headquarters of the League of Nations in Geneva, built between 1929 and 1936. Since 1946 it has housed the United Nations Office at Geneva and is a regular venue for negotiations on peace, disarmament and human rights.
